#3494. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3493. Marshals Season 2 Episode 6 Is Based On A Tragic Real-Life Story

"Marshals" has had its share of problems, but its latest chapter manages to deliver an emotionally powerful storyline based on a real-life tragedy. Season 2, Episode 6, "Roughstock," sees Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton investigating the death of Mo's (Mo Brings Plenty) nephew, Troy (Will Strongheart), in a storyline based on the real death of Mo Brings Plenty's 27-year-old nephew, Cole Brings Plenty.

Backing up a bit: "Marshals" Season 1 solidified why the pitched Thomas Rainwater (Gil Birmingham) spin-off needs to exist. In lieu of that series, Grimes' procedural has at least given Rainwater and the Broken Rock reservation significant attention so far. Not only that, the "Yellowstone" spin-off has tried to highlight real-life issues faced by Native American communities, such as in the Season 1 episode that saw Kayce and the Marshals tracking down trafficked Broken Rock girls. Now, Season 2, Episode 6 has gone even further by using the passing of Mo's nephew as the basis for its narrative.

Cole Brings Plenty was found dead in April 2024 near Kansas City, Kansas, having been reported missing a few days prior. An actor, Cole previously played Pete Plenty Clouds in the "Yellowstone" prequel "1923" and appeared in an episode of "The Tall Tales of Jim Bridger" and four episodes of "Into the Wild Frontier." Prior to the discovery of his body, police identified Cole as a suspect in a domestic violence incident. After the actor was confirmed as having passed away, The Johnson County Sheriff's Office determined there was "no indication of foul play." But the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe quickly demanded a "full and thorough investigation into Cole's disappearance and subsequent death." Hence, in "Roughstock," Kayce takes it upon himself to carry out such an investigation into Troy's death.

"Marshals" Season 2 started in disappointing fashion, but "Roughstock" marks its best episode yet. In this chapter, Kayce Dutton and Mo Brings Plenty search for Mo's nephew, Troy, before discovering his body at the foot of a cliff. There, a police officer dismisses the death as suicide and warns Kayce and Mo not to investigate further. They don't listen. Instead, they mount a search for more clues alongside Andrea Cruz (Ash Santos) and Miles Kittle (Tatanka Means). This leads them to a group of poachers, one of whom recalls seeing an as yet unidentified man hit Troy with a flashlight prior to his cliff fall, thus confirming there was more to Troy's passing than police claimed.

For Mo Brings Plenty, highlighting this issue of police failing to investigate the suspicious deaths of Native Americans was important, especially since he had a personal connection to the story. In a TVLine interview, the actor said he was "very thankful" to showrunner Spencer Hudnut and his writers for "Roughstock," explaining, "My brother and I shared our real-life experiences with them and explained to them what occurred, and for them to take that and then create this beautiful storyline and give us, give me the opportunity to share that, I'm just so thankful."

"Roughstock" ends with a service to Troy, after which Mo carries out his own ritual by a fire, bidding his nephew farewell before seeing a white horse appear in a field. As the actor told TVLine, "Here, he has his own moment to clear himself and to be able to see the other side. That was the symbolism of the horse. It represented the other side, and Mo knows that his nephew made it, because I know that my real nephew Cole made it."

As of now, Troy's killer remains unidentified. No doubt, the Marshals will continue to pursue justice for Mo Brings Plenty's nephew. For now, though, it's interesting to see "Marshals" take such a direct approach to representing Native Americans. "Yellowstone" featured several storylines designed to highlight issues faced by Indigenous tribes, and "Marshals" has maintained that aspect of its mothership series. But this is the first time the show has taken a real-life story and adapted it so directly. If nothing else, it adds a little more depth to a series that has thus far struggled to achieve any sense of believability.

"Marshals" has no idea what it's about, and that shows no signs of changing after the first six episodes of Season 2. Even Episode 6, its respectful adaptation of a real-life event is otherwise full of stilted dialogue and performances that leave a lot to be desired. "Roughstock" has the series' signature paroxysms of melodrama as well, such as when an Army veteran suddenly pulls a gun in a parking lot, forcing Pete Calvin (Logan Marshall-Green) and Belle Skinner (Arielle Kebel) to hurriedly diffuse the situation. It's a shame, really, given the rest of the episode does a decent and respectful job of highlighting a real-world tragedy.

Meanwhile, USA Today reports that the Johnson County Sheriff's Office claimed to have "conducted a thorough investigation" into Cole Brings Plenty's death and that the findings had been presented to the family. But Mo Brings Plenty and the family remain unsatisfied. "When the wheel of justice doesn't turn for us," Brings Plenty told the outlet, "I know it didn't for us, and I know there are a lot of families that are in the same situation as we are."

Johnny Depp is officially back in Hollywood, at least as far as his career is concerned. His 2026 movie release, Ebenezer, just topped the domestic box office, marking his first major studio release in eight years. But while the actor is making his way back onto movie screens (even for lesser pay), he's apparently in no hurry to return to living in the United States. In fact, he's been spending most of his time somewhere that sounds an awful lot like a vacation destination.

The Pirates of the Caribbean star recently spoke with The Wall Street Journal about his childhood, his unlikely introduction to acting and where he calls home these days. I knew Depp owned an island in the Bahamas, but I hadn't realized just how much time he actually spends there. According to the 63-year-old actor:

Today, I live most of the time in the Bahamas. It’s where I’ve found total peace and quiet. Nobody's pointing a camera at me or staring.

I suppose having your own island makes avoiding the paparazzi considerably easier. And considering how much attention Depp's personal life has received over the years, I can understand why he'd want somewhere he can go about his day without somebody pointing a camera at him.

Yet what I found particularly interesting was how the Oscar nominee described the property itself. Depp purchased Little Hall's Pond Cay, a 45-acre island in the Bahamas, in 2004 for a reported $3.6 million. And while I pictured some enormous Caribbean mansion, his description of the place sounds surprisingly modest. He continued:

I bought my 1940s wood house in 2004 and added a yurt and a painting studio. Art continues to be a sanctuary that lets me process the world around me.

A wooden house, a yurt and somewhere to paint. Not exactly what I would have pictured for the man who spent years playing one of Disney's most recognizable characters, but I can appreciate the appeal.

Depp also told the publication that he enjoys reading and playing guitar in his music studio, which sounds about right for somebody who originally moved to Los Angeles hoping to make it as a musician.

Forget Scrooge, Johnny Depp Will Soon Be Back On The Big Screen For What May Be His Scariest Role Ever

His current living situation is especially interesting considering how frequently his family moved when he was growing up. Depp recalled relocating approximately 40 times during his childhood, particularly after his family moved from Kentucky to Florida. The constant changes made it difficult to settle in, and he described himself as an outsider.

Music eventually became his escape. His mother gave him an acoustic guitar when he was 12, and by 1983, Depp had moved to Los Angeles with his band, hoping to make a career out of playing music. Then he met Nicolas Cage.

According to Depp, the two became friends after Cage started attending his band's performances. Eventually, Cage suggested that he try acting and helped connect him with an agent. That led to his film debut in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street, followed by the career that made him one of Hollywood's biggest stars.

Of course, his relationship with Hollywood became considerably more complicated in recent years. Depp stepped away from major American studio productions amid legal battles with his ex-wife, Amber Heard, including their highly publicized 2022 defamation trial. He continued working internationally, appearing in the French film Jeanne du Barry and directing Modi: Three Days on the Wing of Madness.

Now, he's back with Ti West's Ebenezer, which opened Nov. 13 and earned an estimated $19 million domestically during its first weekend. But does the box-office win signal a larger Hollywood comeback? Only time will tell, but Depp has another major American release on the horizon: Day Drinker, a thriller co-starring Penélope Cruz, arriving on the 2027 movie schedule. Still, his latest comments suggest returning to American movies doesn't necessarily mean returning to a US address.

The '80s heartthrob has owned his Bahamian retreat for more than two decades, so this isn't some sudden relocation following his Hollywood troubles. But hearing him describe how much time he spends there gives a better idea of what his life looks like these days. After years of playing Jack Sparrow, I suppose it's fitting that Johnny Depp found a little peace on an island of his own.

Ebenezer is now playing in theaters, so check your local listings for showtimes. If you want to revisit Depp's iconic portrayal of Captain Jack, all the Pirates of the Caribbean films stream with a Disney+ subscription.

#3490. ‘Ghosts’ Season 6 Is Taking an Unnecessary Risk With Its Release Formula

Comedy fans have been wondering when Ghosts will return for Season 6, and now they have their answer. Following a pair of holiday specials, the supernatural comedy will return in January 2027 in its usual time slot. However, there's a major change to its release schedule: the show will now air twice-weekly. In addition to its regular Thursday slot, Ghosts will also air episodes on Mondays following Eternally Yours. While this is an attempt to build a block of supernatural comedy programming, it might be a majorly wrong move on CBS's part.

For starters, shifting to a twice-weekly schedule will disrupt the series' steady momentum. Part of the fun of watching Ghosts is seeing how Jay (Utkarsh Ambudkar) and Sam (Rose McIver), alongside Kyle (Ben Feldman), run a bed-and-breakfast full of ghosts. Though the holiday specials and certain episodes have been two-part stories, they've usually aired on a single night. Shifting that status would erase the steady pacing that's made Ghosts a breakout series, and in an age when it's one of the few network series still commanding a steady audience, that could be a death sentence.

Instead of one night to sit back, relax, and catch up on new episodes, the schedule shift for Ghosts means fans risk missingan episode. That could lead to falling behind on the series and missing key developments or a genuinely funny moment — or worse, both. While streaming services have given fans more access to certain series, part of the joy of watching Ghosts lies in catching it live. Doubling the number of episodes could lead fans not only to fall behind, but eventually to skip watching altogether and wait for the entire season to drop on Paramount+.

That's a lapse that CBS can't afford. Ghosts's viewership has fluctuated over the years, as it started out strong but has decreased slightly with each season. Shifting to two episodes a week could hurt those ratings, and given that Ghosts is still one of CBS's highest-rated series, it feels like a risky gamble. Ghosts is also preparing to take some of its biggest swings yet, as Rebecca Wisocky recently told Collider that the upcoming Christmas special will be a major game changer:

"Lots of people are in peril. The stakes are perhaps the highest that they have ever been. And I don't say that lightly."

If Ghosts lives up to Wisocky's words, this won't be a season to miss. Not only will the show hit its milestone 100th episode, but the new dynamic between Jay and Kyle makes for a fresh start. Doubling up on episodes risks burning through these interesting developments, but CBS might have a good reason beyond filling up its schedule.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Some people might ask why Ghosts is doubling up on episodes, and the answer lies in another upcoming event that dominates CBS's schedule. "March Madness" will see the network air college basketball games throughout March and April, a period when multiple series usually go on hiatus until the tournament ends. If Ghosts does a double-header of its own, it could build up to a mid-season hiatus and air the rest of its episodes through May, when its season finales usually debut. This could also mark a shift back to single episodes, depending on how viewers receive Ghosts' twice-weekly episodes.

Ghosts stands out in the modern television landscape not just because it's a great comedy, but also because it sticks to a set of rules most TV shows have abandoned. It's managed to (mostly) stick to the 22-episode order that most audiences feel is outdated, and has won over an audience thanks to its mix of humor and supernatural tropes. By altering the release schedule, CBS is losing sight of what makes the series worth watching.

Seasons 1–5 of Ghosts are available to stream on Paramount+.

#3488. What Ebenezer's Box Office Means For Johnny Depp's Hollywood Future

Johnny Depp was once one of cinema's most cherished mainstream actors. From his early successes like "Edward Scissorhands" to Oscar-nominated blockbusters like "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl," he seemed unstoppable. It all came crashing down in the late 2010s but now, Depp is back with "Ebenezer." And based on the movie's early box office returns, it looks like his Hollywood comeback may be the real deal. At the very least, it's not over yet.

Directed by Ti West ("X," "Pearl"), "Ebenezer" opened to $19 million at the domestic box office, taking the number one spot on the charts. While "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office on its opening weekend, it dropped 72% for an $8.5 million second frame. That paved the way for Depp's new take on Ebenezer Scrooge to take the crown. Internationally, the movie pulled in a further $23 million, giving it a $42 million global start.

Against a reported $38 million production budget, that makes this an instant winner for Paramount Pictures, especially since Christmas movies tend to hang around during the holiday season. Not to mention that they also tend to have especially long lives beyond the box office. All of this to say, it looked like "Ebenezer" might be the box office hit that Depp's Hollywood comeback needed and it proved out.

The movie is based on Charles Dickens' "A Christmas Carol" but promises a new take on the familiar tale. "If you think you know his story, think again," the tagline boasts. It boasts a star-studded cast that also includes Rupert Grint, Daisy Ridley, and Ian McKellen, among many others.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is going to be a bigger hit than people realize, taking up a lot of oxygen this upcoming weekend. Thanksgiving brings with it even more competition from Disney's "Hexed" and "Focker In-Law." That said, if "Ebenezer" holds even decently well, Johnny Depp has a real shot at a meaningful Hollywood comeback, with some caveats.

For one, this is going to be a mid-budget, decent hit. It's going to build a bridge, but not a terribly sturdy one. After all of the fallout from the much-publicized feud between Depp and his ex-wife Amber Heard, many studios may still be reluctant to work with him. However, it's clear the general public is willing to turn up for a Depp-fronted motion picture.

#3484. Samara Weaving's Gritty Crime Thriller Is One Of Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hits

Samara Weaving is one of the most charismatic young actresses working right now. She's got one of the most expressive acting faces this side of Saoirse-Monica Jackson in "Derry Girls," and the comic sense to know how to use it.

2026 has been good for Weaving — and not just because she booked a part as Emma Frost in Marvel Studios' upcoming "X-Men" movie. This past year, Weaving has starred in three movies. She returned for a sequel to her 2019 horror movie "Ready or Not," and co-starred with Jason Segel in "Over Your Dead Body," a comedy-thriller about two spouses plotting to kill each other (like "War of the Roses" with violence out of "Looney Tunes"). The year's third Weaving film is "Carolina Carolina," which came and went from theaters with not even $1 million to its name. But since being added to Netflix on November 6, 2026, the movie has consistently placed in the service's top 10 most viewed movies.

Directed by Adam Carter Rehmeier, "Carolina Caroline" stars Weaving as Caroline Daniels, working as a gas station attendant in Texas at the turn of the millennium. One day, the slick Oliver Anderson (Kyle Gallner) saunters in and tricks the station's cashier out of $20. Carolina, noticing the con, is nonetheless charmed by Oliver. They hit it off, him teaching her how to run short change cons, and, before long, they're driving across the American South robbing banks together. If you've ever heard the names "Bonnie" and "Clyde," then you know what to expect from this story, but familiar pleasures are pleasures nonetheless.

The engine of "Carolina Caroline" is the central criminal romance. Oliver is Caroline's teacher and her lover, and the sexiness of their romance is intertwined with the lawbreaking. The movie never forgets Oliver is the more experienced criminal, making him more ruthless. That he genuinely loves Caroline only hardens him more when facing the rest of the world, especially when their fortunes predictably take a bad turn in the third act. While Caroline is sometimes shocked by the violence, it reads more as inexperience first, conscience second.

The casting helps fuel the movie, too. It'd be overstating it to call "Carolina Caroline" a "Heat"-esque movie star collision. But both Samara Weaving and Kyle Gallner (who previously worked with Adam Carter Rehmeier in 2022's "Dinner in America") are genre favorites. Weaving is a scream queen and horror-action star thanks to "Ready or Not," while Gallner is a frequent face in horror movies, too: "Smile," the subverted slasher "Strange Darling," etc. Pair their charms together, and you never doubt for a second what draws Caroline and Oliver to risk it all in their whirlwind love story.

"Carolina Caroline" prompts comparisons to New Hollywood movies about fugitive lovers, including not just "Bonnie & Clyde" but also Terence Malick's "Badlands." Like those movies (released in 1967 and 1973, respectively), "Carolina Caroline" sets itself a couple decades in the past for a more nostalgic feeling. The movie doesn't even immediately scan as a period piece until you notice that no-one has a cell phone. With its indeterminate late 90s/early 2000s setting, "Carolina Caroline" stakes itself in the last decade that a story about criminals pulling big jobs then staying anonymous for months afterwards could happen.

"Carolina Caroline" is streaming on Netflix.

#3483. Marvel's Vision Was Originally Intended As A Revival Of A Forgotten Superhero

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Since his introduction in 2015's "Avengers: Age of Ultron," the Vision (Paul Bettany) has become one of the most enduring Marvel Cinematic Universe characters. Not even getting his vibranium head crushed by Thanos (Josh Brolin) back in "Avengers: Infinity War" stopped him from returning in the TV series "WandaVision" — in which Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) conjures the life she wanted with Vision — and "VisionQuest," which revisits Vision's relationship with Ultron (James Spader), his "father."

Created by Roy Thomas and John Buscema, Vision debuted in 1968's "The Avengers" issue #57. Unlike in the MCU, where Ultron creates Vision's "synthezoid" body for himself before the Avengers steal it, comic Ultron (then known as Ultron-5) created Vision as a conscious being to lure the Avengers to their doom. Vision then turned against his creator, and the following issue #58 saw him inaugurated as an Avenger.

But Vision as we know him almost didn't exist. Thomas is a fan of the "Golden Age of Comics," aka the earliest period of superhero comics in the 1940s. Back then, Marvel was called Timely Comics, and its superhero stable included Aarkus, an interdimensional being named The Vision. Created in 1940 by Joe Simon and Jack Kirby (the same year that they created Captain America), the Vision debuted in "Marvel Mystery" #13. Summoned to Earth by scientist Enoch Mason, Aarkus hails from a supernatural dimension called "Smokeworld."

Originally, Thomas wanted to bring back this Vision as an Avenger, as Stan Lee and Kirby had brought back Captain America in "Avengers" #4. But Lee (without giving a reason) insisted on an android hero instead, so Thomas and Buscema created a new Vision in the image of the 1940s one. Aarkus has made occasional reappearances, but he definitely sits in the shadow of the later Vision.

Roy Thomas, who wrote "The Avengers" from issue #35 through #104, sometimes felt like he was playing in the minor leagues. Speaking to Yahoo in 2015, Thomas recounted: "Stan [Lee] kept taking Captain America, Iron Man, and Thor away from the Avengers. Every few months I would request to bring them back to the fold. I would say, 'You left me with a bunch of losers here.'"

When looking for a new Avenger, Thomas wanted to revive the Golden Age Vision because "[he] didn't like to create new characters for Marvel, because [he] wouldn't own them."

Vision's origin honored Lee's request to make the new Avenger an android, but Thomas and John Buscema's Vision still looks a lot like Aarkus. They share a mostly green color scheme, a high collar cape, a bald head, etc. Vision's intangibility powers also evoke Aarkus appearing and disappearing in plumes of smoke. There are some different details, granted. Vision has a "solar gem" on his forehead (which Thomas credits to Buscema, and which the MCU tweaked into one of the Infinity Stones), as well as red skin (unlike Aarkus' pale green).

Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter in 2015, Thomas surmised that Lee wasn't totally satisfied with the Vision, noting he disliked the hero's red color ("Red's not a good color!") and the "Vision" name. "It seems a little wimpy, but I felt Vision — it really means like a ghost or a mirage or an image," Thomas explained.

Nonetheless, history shows Vision's creation came with a huge ripple effect, reshaping "The Avengers" forever. Many of the book's core storylines go back to Vision, like his romance with the Scarlet Witch or Ultron's persistent efforts to destroy the Avengers, his son included.

Ultron debuted only a few issues before Vision, in "Avengers" #54. Issue #57 saw Vision seemingly destroy his creator, while issue #58 revealed the Avenger Hank Pym/Ant-Man had created Ultron, leading to the robot rebelling and erasing his creator's memory. Roy Thomas told Yahoo, "I knew right away [Ultron] is a character you would bring back." So he did when, in "Avengers" #66, subliminal programming inside Vision makes him restore Ultron in a new adamantium body. As for Vision and the Scarlet Witch, Thomas told Syfy in 2022 that he paired them because Vision didn't have a solo title, so Thomas had sole control over Vision's story.

If Aarkus the Vision had become an Avenger, it's plausible he'd have filled a superficially similar role on the team. Perhaps he and Wanda would've even ended up together. But he'd lack the connection to Ultron, which would diminish the villain.

In a foreword to 2015's "Avengers: Rage of Ultron," former "Avengers" writer Kurt Busiek notes the Ultron-Vision thread running through "Avengers" is a family saga. The family theme also heightens the contradictions that make Ultron more than just a killer robot. He's literally inhuman, yet he behaves more like an angry and erratic child than a cold machine, closer to Frankenstein's Creature than Hal 9000.

This makes Thomas and John Buscema creating Vision, instead of resurrecting Aarkus, a lynchpin moment of entertainment history in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Stan Lee, Thomas, and Buscema, when pumping out cheaply-printed "Avengers" comics in the 1960s and '70s, could've hardly predicted Vision would be a major character in the biggest blockbuster property ever. Nor that an entire TV series would rest on Vision and Wanda's romance, and then another on Vision and Ultron's antagonistic bond.

#3482. 10 Classic Rock Songs That Will Make Your Thanksgiving Playlist Unforgettable

Thanksgiving means a lot of different things to different people, but there are a few universal themes that can't be ignored. There's family, there's gratitude, and there's good food. Some people will have their favorite artists to accompany them during special, but for those who are still looking for inspiration, we got you covered.

It's normal to go through many moods during a long family dinner. If you haven't seen them for a long time, it's bound to be emotional. If you're used to seeing them, chances are there will be a lot of laughter and joking around. And of course, it wouldn't be Thanksgiving without a huge dinner that leaves you panting. The Beatles, John Denver, Led Zeppelin, and many more artists and bands have created the perfect songs for your Thanksgiving playlist, and we have put them together.

We're opening this list with the most famous rock-country anthem, "Take Me Home, Country Roads," also known simply as "Country Roads." Who hasn't belted this beautiful track at the top of their lungs with a huge grin? Written by John Denver, Bill Danoff, and Taffy Nivert, and released on Denver's 1971 album, Poems, Prayers and Promises, it perfectly embodies the spirit of togetherness, gratitude, and belonging.

While it was John Denver who made it popular, the first draft of the song was originally written by Bill Danoff and Taffy Nivert. The songwriters were a couple, and were looking for a home for this song. At first, Danoff explained, they were hesitant to give it to John Denver, since they felt it might not be his style, but Denver not only loved it but helped make it into the great track it is. When asked if they regretted "giving away" their greatest hit, Danoff waved it off.

"Left to our own devices, Taffy and I may have never gotten that record cut," Danoff admitted. "It wasn't a country record. We could've beat up Nashville and nobody would've recorded it. One thing I learned in this business is that things turn out other than you planned them to, no matter what it is. And you can't predict what's going to happen." Besides, they're still credited as songwriters, so they took a big paycheck home anyway.

The title alone would earn this Led Zeppelin song a spot on the Thanksgiving playlist, but the content, despite not being strictly about the holiday, makes "Thank You" sound like it was made for Thanksgiving. It was written by Robert Plant for his first wife, Maureen Wilson. "Kind woman, I give you my all / Kind woman, nothing more," he promises in the song. "And so today, my world it smiles / Your hand in mine, we walk the miles / Thanks to you it will be done / For you to me are the only one."

Plant's relationship with Wilson is deeply romantic yet tragic. The couple were married for 14 years before splitting up, and they went through everything together. They had three children, and their middle child tragically passed away at five years old. Despite splitting up, they remained friends, and while the song might have changed meaning through the years, it never stopped being true.

The ultimate song about loving your homeland, "Sweet Home Alabama" was Lynyrd Skynyrd's response to Neil Young's songs about slavery, like "Alabama" and "Southern Man." The band felt that those songs painted an unfair picture of the modern Southern culture, so they decided to write a rebuttal about their love for their state.

"Big wheels keep on turning / Carry me home to see my kin / Singing songs about the Southland / I miss Alabamy once again and I think it's a sin, yes," the song opens. Young is even name-checked later on in the track. "Well, I heard Mister Young sing about her (southern man) / Well, I heard ol' Neil put her down / Well, I hope Neil Young will remember / A southern man don't need him around, anyhow."

But despite the diss part of the song, the underlying message is perfect for Thanksgiving. Returning to where you belong to spend time with the people you love, and being grateful for the chance to go back. "Sweet home Alabama / Where the skies are so blue / Sweet home Alabama / Lord, I'm coming home to you."

"Harvest Moon," from Neil Young's album by the same name, is one of his most famous and beloved tracks. A song about celebrating life and treasuring the time with your loved ones, "Harvest Moon" is an essential part of any Thanksgiving playlist. "Come a little bit closer / Hear what I have to say / Just like children sleepin' / We could dream this night away," he sings. It's a song about the passage of time and how love prevails, and the full moon is used as a metaphor for tradition and endurance. "Because I'm still in love with you / I want to see you dance again / Because I'm still in love with you / On this harvest moon." Perfect for the most moving moments of a family holiday, as it's guaranteed to make you reflect and appreciate your time with your loved ones more.

Another song about coming home, which is a recurrent topic for the holidays. After all, holidays are, at their core, an excuse to come home. "Homeward Bound" is one of Simon & Garfunkel's most famous songs, and partly that's because of the universal feeling of the lyrics. "I'm sittin' in the railway station / Got a ticket for my destination / On a tour of one-night stands / My suitcase and guitar in hand / And every stop is neatly planned / For a poet and a one-man band," they sing wistfully. In the song, however, the narrator is not taking the train to go home. He just wishes he was. "Homeward bound / I wish I was / Homeward bound / Home where my thought's escapin' / Home where my music's playin' / Home where my love lies waitin' / Silently for me," they sing in the chorus.

The lyrics are about a very real memory. Paul Simon remembers sitting down at a train station in Liverpool when he was just 22. A young artist trying to make his way into the world, away from home, feeling homesick. What's more relatable than that?

A classic folk rock song that is perfect for the whole family to sing along. It's pretty long, has plenty of verses, and a fun, easy chorus that makes it great to sing along to, especially later on in the evening. The most surprising thing about "The Weight" is that it was created almost accidentally. Written by guitarist Robbie Robertson, it was considered a "back-up" song, since Robertson wrote it while trying to overcome writer's block.

“I played it for the other guys, to get this thing started,” Robertson explained. “And everybody was like, ‘Hell, well that sounds pretty good!’ And I said,‘Well, it’ll just be a back-up song in case some other things don’t work out.’” To this day, it's The Band's greatest song.

"Savoy Truffle," from The Beatles' legendary White Album, is an often overlooked George Harrison composition, and it's perfect for the Thanksgiving feast. In fact, Harrison wrote it about the risks of gorging on sweets. He allegedly wrote it for his best friend, Eric Clapton, to warn him about his "chocolate addiction," and it matches the feeling of overeating during the holidays.

"Creme tangerine and Montelimar / A ginger sling with a pineapple heart / Coffee dessert, yes, you know it's good news / But you'll have to have them all pulled out / After the Savoy truffle," Harrison sings, before warning about the side effects in the bridge: "You might not feel it now / But when the pain cuts through / You're going to know and how / The sweat is going to fill your head / When it becomes too much / You'll shout aloud."

A beautiful love song, and often considered the best song by the Beach Boys, "God Only Knows" should start playing towards the moment when the family is going around sharing what they are thankful for. It's a song about appreciation and unconditional love, and it never fails to bring tears to people's eyes. "I may not always love you / But as long as there are stars above you / You never need to doubt it / I'll make you so sure about it / God only knows what I'd be without you," Brian Wilson promises on this timeless anthem.

"Two of Us" is the opening track of the controversial final album by The Beatles, Let It Be. It's a soft, upbeat folksy ballad that Paul McCartney wrote about his adventures with his first wife, Linda McCartney, and it's about exploring and having fun with your partner, and the beauty of always going home with them at the end of the day.

"You and I have memories / Longer than the road that stretches out ahead," McCartney promises in the song. "Two of us wearing raincoats / Standing solo in the sun / You and me chasing paper / Getting nowhere on our way back home."

"Our House" by Crosby, Stills, Nash, & Young is a song about domestic bliss that every young family should absolutely add to their Thanksgiving playlist, especially if it's their first time hosting. This track, written by Graham Nash, is about his love story with another rockstar, Joni Mitchell, and an epiphany he had during an ordinary day watching her pick up flowers in their garden.

"Our house is a very, very, very fine house / With two cats in the yard / Life used to be so hard / Now everything is easy 'cause of you," Nash sings happily. It's a song about the beauty of everyday things, and it's perfect for a day of giving thanks.

#3481. Netflix Officially Confirms 3 Body Problem Returns in 2027

Season 2 of the ambitious thriller is nearly finally here

Netflix's long-awaited second season of 3 Body Problem finally has a release date. The streamer announced Monday that season 2 of the sci-fi series, an adaptation of author Cixin Liu's Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy, will arrive on Jan. 14, 2027. That's nearly three years after the first season of 3 Body Problem debuted on Netflix.

3 Body Problem co-creators, writers, and executive producers David Benioff, D.B. Weiss, and Alexander Woo explain why the second season has taken so long: It's the scope.

"The tone really changes once you get to the second season," the trio said in a statement on Netflix's Tudum blog. "It’s much bigger. Things get wilder, the conflicts get more cosmic. Once people see it on the screen, they’re going to understand why we’ve been so excited for this season, in particular."

The first season of 3 Body Problem adapted Liu's first book The Three-Body Problem (and elements of its sequels), with seasons 2 and 3 presumably adapting the remainder, The Dark Forest and Death's End. The Three-Body Problem was relatively grounded in human stories compared to the expansive interstellar war explored in Liu's second and third entries in the Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy.

Fortunately, it appears we'll get the entire cerebral sci-fi series; Netflix renewed 3 Body Problem for seasons 2 and 3 back in May 2024.

Season 1 of 3 Body Problem stars Jovan Adepo, John Bradley, Rosalind Chao, Liam Cunningham, Eiza González, Jess Hong, Marlo Kelly, Alex Sharp, Sea Shimooka, Zine Tseng, Saamer Usmani, Benedict Wong, and Jonathan Pryce. Season 2 will add new series regulars Claudia Doumit (The Boys) as Captain Van Rijn and Ellie de Lange (Wolf Hall) as Ayla. Alfie Allen (Game of Thrones), David Yip (The Chinese Detective), and Jordan Sunshine (The Pitt) are set for recurring roles.

The first season of 3 Body Problem ends on a pretty dour note. The hostile San-Ti are headed to Earth. The Project Staircase experiment — in which the cryogenically frozen brain of Will Downing is being sent into space — has failed. After multiple assassination attempts, Saul Durand has accepted becoming a Wallfacer and is conceiving a mental plan to defeat the San-Ti. Auggie Salazar has gone off the grid.

Faced with a down-on-its-luck crew, Benedict Wong's detective, Da Shi, tries to rally the surviving members of the Oxford Five by ... comparing humanity to cicadas. "People hate bugs, been trying to get rid of them forever,” Da Shi tells them, reminding them that the San-Ti view humanity as nothing more than bugs. “Look around, they’re not going anywhere.”

#3480. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3479. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3478. After Gilligan's Island, Jim Backus And Alan Hale Jr. Reunited On A Legendary Western Series

"Gilligan's Island" might have been a silly slapstick sitcom, but it remains beloved even almost 60 years after it went off the air. Of course, after the third and final season, the castaways managed to keep themselves in the public consciousness via a syndication deal, two animated "Gilligan's Island" spin-offs, and three TV movies — and that's to say nothing of the unofficial reunions.

Members of the "Gilligan's Island" cast re-teamed on numerous projects in the years after the show proper went off the air. In fact, Captain Jonas Grumby and Thurston Howell III actors Alan Hale Jr. and Jim Backus couldn't wait to get back on-set together. The pair reunited a couple years after the castaways bid viewers farewell, when they both appeared in one of the best classic Western series: "The Wild Wild West."

This legendary show famously combined the sci-fi, spy, and Western genres to create a unique experience, which ran for four seasons on the network that also hosted "Gilligan's Island," CBS. "The Wild Wild West" debuted in September 1965, the same month the castaways returned for their second season. By 1969, however, "Gilligan's Island" had been off the air for two years while "The Wild Wild West" was entering its fourth and final season (though it, too, would live on via TV movies and an infamous big screen reimagining). It was during this final run that Hale Jr. and Backus both appeared in the episode "The Night of the Sabatini Death."

"The Wild Wild West" debuted at a time when the sci-fi genre was already beginning to supercede the Western. It ultimately took until the mid-'70s for Old West adventures to fall out of favor completely (though, if you'd have asked Roger Ebert he would have said 2001's Ali Larter-led "American Outlaws" finally killed the Western for good). Before the decline of this once beloved genre began in earnest, however, Michael Garrison conceived of a series which he famously envisioned as "James Bond on horseback." But that was only part of the "Wild Wild West" formula.

The show, set in the post-Civil war era, followed Secret Service agents James West (Robert Conrad) and Artemus Gordon (Ross Martin), who thwarted all manner of threat to the United States using advanced technology. That added a sci-fi element to the show's melding of the Western and spy genres, making it a triple threat that immediately proved popular. By the time Alan Hale, Jr. and Jim Backus guested, the show was well-established as a small screen favorite, even while CBS was preparing to drop the axe.

"The Night of the Sabatini Death" begins with dying crime boss Johnny Sabatini (Ted de Corsia) meeting Jim West. It seems the sickly kingpin wants West to ensure his niece, Caroline (Sylvia Nolan), receives a gift he's leaving her. West then travels to Calliope, Missouri, alongside his new agent colleague (Ross Martin was missing from several Season 4 episodes) Ned Brown, who's played by Hale Jr. In Calliope, West meets mortician Fabian Swanson (Backus) who is dispatched halfway through the episode, becoming a "customer of his own establishment" as West puts it.

At the end of "The Night of the Sabatini Death" Alan Hale Jr.'s Ned Brown departs, telling James West he plans to "spend a vacation all alone on a desert island." The "Gilligan's Island" theme then plays, confirming this is, indeed, a nod to Hale's Skipper role (poor old Jim Backus doesn't get to do anything near as fun).

Interestingly enough, Hale Jr. and Backus' appearance in "The Night of the Sabatini Death" was far from the only link between "Gilligan's Island" and "The Wild Wild West." Dawn Wells, who'd played Mary Ann Summers on the CBS sitcom also appeared on "The Wild Wild West" the year prior to her former co-stars. The actress guest starred in the 1968 episode "The Night of the Headless Woman," playing Betsy Jeffers, daughter of Richard Anderson's Commissioner James Jeffers. It was a brief appearance, but it meant she beat her "Gilligan's Island' colleagues to the series.

What's more, "The Wild Wild West" was one of many shows to make use of "Gilligan's Island" sets, most notably the lagoon which had been built on the CBS Studios backlot. "Gilligan's Island" also shared this set with "Gunsmoke," the show which ultimately forced the sitcom off the air. But it also came in handy for the adventures of James West and Artemus Gordon.

Sadly, those adventures came to an end shortly after Hale and Backus' guest appearances on the show. "The Wild Wild West" was ultimately canceled to appease a Congress eager to prove it was against violence in every form, including the small screen variety. Today, we can at least see Hale Jr. and Backus' "Wild Wild West" guest spots for free on Pluto TV.

#3476. Batman Forever's Director Nearly Rejected Jim Carrey As The Riddler Until He Saw This Movie

Say what you will about the "Batman" movies of the 1990s, there's no denying that they brought some truly massive star power to the screen. Even "Batman and Robin," often derided as the worst film of the entire franchise, was loaded with A-list actors, including Arnold Schwarzenegger, Uma Thurman, Alicia Silverstone, and a cameo appearance by the rapper Coolio. It was 1995's "Batman Forever," though, that gave the series what was arguably its biggest casting coup, when director Joel Schumacher cast Jim Carrey as the Riddler.

At the time, Carrey was experiencing a meteoric rise thanks to the success of "Ace Ventura: Pet Detective" and "Dumb and Dumber," which both released in 1994 and propelled him to the role of one of Hollywood's most prominent comedic actors. Looking back, putting him opposite Schumacher's campier Caped Crusader seems like a natural fit. Initially, however, Schumacher thought Carrey was simply too young to play the part. As revealed in a 1994 interview with "Comics Scene," the director only changed his mind when he saw Carrey bring another comic book to life on the big scree. As Carrey told the magazine, Schumacher "thought I was a little too young. Then, when he saw the trailer for 'The Mask,' he changed his mind."

While it went through some significant changes on its way to becoming a film — mostly to tone down the violence that made director Chuck Russell initially think of it as a horror movie and add in way more swing dancing — "The Mask" started out as a comic book by writer John Arcudi and artist Doug Mahnke. Carrey, whose over-the-top delivery and exaggerated impressions made him a breakout star on the sketch comedy show "In Living Color," was the perfect fit for the cartoonish, chaotic madman that emerged when the power of the trickster god Loki wound up in the hands of a relatively lovable loser.

Although he allegedly had a much longer cut of the film that skewed darker and more serious than the final result, Schumacher's take on Batman was heavily influenced by the 1960s TV show, so it makes sense that he'd look for a comic actor to play the Riddler. Long before the Riddler was the dark and murderous villain of "The Batman," he was one of the Dark Knight's sillier foes. Frank Gorshin, who played the Riddler to perfection on that show, was a well-known comedian and impressionist himself, and before Carrey's casting, Robin Williams was considered to be a favorite for the part. Seeing Carrey pull off the menacing silliness of "The Mask" and make that film a huge hit likely did a lot to sell Schumacher on giving Carrey a chance — and the fact that Carrey did it while wearing a lot of green probably didn't hurt either.

As for how it worked out, well, Carrey's performance as Edward Nygma in "Batman Forever" was, to put it charitably, a lot. The Riddler was undoubtedly annoying on purpose, but Carrey into being straight-up grating. Even his co-star thought so, with Tommy Lee Jones (who played Two-Face in the film) famously telling him "I cannot sanction your buffoonery" when they met.

That said, there are some really great parts of his performance, too. While the Riddler was way over the top, the way Carrey plays Edward Nygma as an obsessive fanboy of Val Kilmer's Bruce Wayne, including a scene where he dresses like Wayne down to the glasses while showing off his mind-controlling invention, is actually really solid. It's also the kind of subtle — well, subtle for Carrey, at least — touch that only really worked because of Carrey's youth.

#3475. My Hero Academia Officially Returns December 9

My Hero Academia ended in May 2026 with the conclusion of its anime run. It was an epic finale, one teeming with the high-octane action that had peppered the rest of the series and popularized the original manga, as well as the tear-jerking sincerity that makes MHA so special. Naturally, with such a phenomenal farewell, fans are eager to see it return, a curse of great endings that remind you why you fell in love with a piece of art in the first place. Fortunately, while MHA is over, a plethora of My Hero Academia spin-off projects have been released.

From the ongoing My Hero Academia: Vigilantes (which fans hope will get a third season) to the recently released third My Hero Academia video game, All's Justice, fans have been treated to a smattering of exciting new projects that have helped keep the spirit of the legendary manga alive. Adding to this pantheon of great MHA content is a brand-new release, one that is set to see fan-favorite characters reborn in an unexpected way.

It turns out that the recently released My Hero Academia Switch 2 game was not the series' final foray into the world of video games, as it is getting a huge crossover event with the popular Ubisoft-published 2D platform fighting game, Brawlhalla. For those not in the know, Brawlhalla was released back in 2017 as a free-to-play platform fighter akin to the Super Smash Bros. series. Its developer, Blue Mammoth Games, was acquired by Ubisoft a year later in 2018, and since then it has served as an excellent and crossover-heavy fighting title that's available across all platforms, including mobile.

This My Hero Academia crossover joins a long line of similar events for other IPs, including WWE, Adventure Time, Hellboy, Rayman, Ben 10, The Walking Dead, and more. This time, fan-favorite characters Midoriya, Bakugo, and Todoroki, as well as a handful of other currently undisclosed characters, are heading into the arena to join the abundance of other existing original and IP-based characters. The event will happen across all platforms, meaning no one will miss out on the opportunity to beat up Ben 10 as Midoriya.

Like previous Brawlhalla crossover events, the newly added characters will exist as unlockable skins for existing Legends. This means that they'll function exactly the same as the Legends they are ostensibly replacing, including sharing the same stats, weapons, and hitboxes. However, they do get their own roster spot, have their name announced when entering the arena, and unique signature effects that help differentiate them from the other characters.

The My Hero Academia characters coming to Brawlhalla have all been reimagined in the game's signature art style so as to better fit alongside the other characters, although they still retain much of their original look. They will be released on December 9 and will be purchasable from the in-game store using the premium currency, Mammoth Coins. If you feel like the existing My Hero Academia fighting games aren't enough, or are a Brawlhalla fan already and want to play as your favorite MHA characters, then this is undeniably the crossover event for you.

#3474. Anne Hathaway's 100-Minute Sci-Fi Thriller Takes Over Streaming After HBO Max Debut

The unusual creature feature has wasted little time finding an audience on streaming

Anne Hathaway has had a particularly busy year, with major projects including Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, the psychological thriller Verity, and the highly anticipated The Devil Wears Prada 2. She's also ventured into more unconventional territory with A24's Mother Mary, a thriller that takes a considerably stranger approach to the world of pop stardom.

The End of Oak Street made its HBO Max debut on Nov. 13 and wasted little time finding an audience. The movie climbed to No. 1 on the platform's U.S. movie chart by Sunday, Nov. 15, according to FlixPatrol's rankings.

Directed by David Robert Mitchell (It Follows, Under the Silver Lake), The End of Oak Street follows the Platt family, whose ordinary suburban life is turned upside down after a mysterious cosmic event transports their entire neighborhood to an unfamiliar location.

Suddenly separated from the world they know, the family discovers that their new surroundings are filled with dangerous and unusual creatures. With their survival at stake, the Platts must work together to navigate their strange new environment and find a way to make it through the ordeal.

Hathaway stars as Denise Platt alongside Ewan McGregor (Star Wars, Trainspotting), Maisy Stella (Nashville) and Christian Convery (Sweet Tooth). Despite its unusual premise, The End of Oak Street has earned a positive reception from critics and audiences. The film currently holds an 86% critics' score and 76% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.

#3473. ‘Doctor Who’ Is Officially Returning, But There’s a Catch

What does the future of Doctor Who look like? It wasn't long ago that a partnership with Disney and the return of showrunner Russell T. Davies left fans feeling as if the show's heyday was on its way back. However, this couldn't be further from the truth, as Davies' return faced poor ratings, mixed fan reception, and the controversial exit of the new titular Time Lord, Ncuti Gatwa. This all culminated in the inevitable shelving of the series, as the BBC put it out to competitive tender earlier this year.

Line of Duty creator Jed Mercurio, through his production company, Hat Trick Mercurio, looks like the favorite to take over the show, with a 2028 or 2029 return rumored. The aforementioned former showrunner, Davies, claimed that a decision on the show would arrive sooner rather than later, saying, "You’ll start to see production with a brand-new Doctor, a brand-new companion, summer next year," in a previous interview. Ahead of that confirmation, Whovians are to be treated to the big-screen return of a fan-favorite episode.

On November 23 and November 28, as part of Doctor Who Day celebrations, The Satan Pit Extended Cut hits theaters in the UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and the U.S. It was already confirmed that the new feature-length edit of the 2006 episodes "The Impossible Planet" and "The Satan Pit" will feature deleted scenes and alternate shots, but now we know that a "specially shot" sequence awaits fans.

"Before the adventure gets underway, audiences will be treated to something specially shot; a lighter, more playful moment featuring a familiar face," reads the latest publication of Doctor Who Magazine, although it is unclear who this "familiar face" is. The screening will also feature an exclusive interview with director James Strong.

The future of Doctor Who might finally be looking up, but former Time Lord Peter Capaldi isn't so positive. The Thick of It star warned in a previous interview that there is only "a small group of professionals" who could take charge of Doctor Who, and that BBC executives who "don't really understand it" threaten to lose what was once so beloved about this sixty-year-old institution. Whatever happens, Whovians will just be glad that their favorite timey-wimey series looks likely to return.

Following a lengthy casting process that, at times, felt like it might never come to an end, Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond. The director of the upcoming 26th Bond installment, Denis Villeneuve, and the new custodian of the 007 franchise, Amazon MGM, have opted for one of the most consistently interesting actors working today, and it will be fascinating to see what the "Primetime" star does as England's greatest spy.

Pattinson's casting as Bond breaks a 60-year tradition of relative unknowns taking on the role. The British actor is one of the biggest stars in the world — which, again, means Amazon MGM shouldn't have to worry too much about box office profits. But he's also one of the most exciting actors of his generation and has been delivering fascinating performances ever since he joined the Safdie Brothers for 2017's "Good Time."

As such, Pattinson's age is surely of little consequence. We know the man can deliver, and everyone should be looking forward to seeing what choices he makes in a role he's described as a "dream come true." But with Amazon MGM likely eyeing a 2028 release date for Pattinson's 007 debut, we've got plenty of time to kill. So, why not take a look at how he measures up to the other Bond actors in terms of age? Here are all the James Bond actors' ages in their first and last 007 movies.

In 1962, "Dr. No kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise," introducing audiences to a rugged young Scotsman by the name of Sean Connery. The actor was born on August 25, 1930, which means he was 31 when filming on "Dr. No" got underway in January 1962. By the time the movie hit theaters in October of that year, he was 32.

Director Terrence Young's urbane manner helped mold Connery's rough-around-the edges Bond into the legendary cinematic figure we remember today. By the time he made his last appearance in the tux for 1971's "Diamonds are Forever," however, he needed no help whatsoever. Filming began in April 1971 when Connery was 40. The film debuted in December of that year, by which point the actor — who passed away in 2020 — was 41, the same age Robert Pattinson will likely be by the time his Bond movie starts shooting. A 52-year-old Connery returned for an unofficial Bond entry in 1983's "Never Say Never Again."

George Lazenby is the only James Bond actor to only appear in the role once. Thankfully, his sole outing as 007 was one of the best Bond movies ever made. 1969's "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" was a brilliant installment in the franchise and is Christopher Nolan's favorite Bond film. Considering Lazenby was following in Sean Connery's footsteps, that's a pretty impressive accomplishment.

Born on September 5, 1939, the Australian model-turned-actor was 29 when filming on "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" began in October 1968. By the time the film debuted in December 1969, Lazenby had turned 30. That was it for the Aussie star, who's still going strong today at the age of 87. "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" was his first and only Bond outing, and Lazenby remains the youngest ever actor to play the role.

After Sean Connery's brief return as James Bond in "Diamonds Are Forever" Roger Moore donned the tux for 1973's "Live and Let Die." The British actor was born on October 14, 1927. Almost exactly 45 years later, his first Bond outing began shooting on October 13, 1972, making him 44 when production started and 45 by the time the movie debuted in June 1973.

That made him older than both Connery and George Lazenby, regardless of whether we're talking their first or last 007 movie. Today, he's still the oldest actor ever cast as James Bond.

Moore retired from the Bond saga with his seventh appearance in the role. He was 57 when "A View to a Kill" bowed in May 1985, and all too aware of his age. The actor told Entertainment Weekly: "I became very conscious that I was getting long in the tooth to play the great lover." More than 40 years later, Moore remains the oldest actor to ever portray Bond.

Next to George Lazenby, Timothy Dalton is surely the most underrated of all the James Bond actors. He brought a darkness to the character long before Daniel Craig's tortured spy debuted, and his interpretation of Bond remains one of the most interesting in the series' history.

The actor was born in Wales on March 21, 1946, making him 40 years old when filming got underway on 1987's "The Living Daylights." When the film opened in July 1987 in the United States, Dalton was 41. He only portrayed Bond in one other film, 1989's "Licence to Kill," and was 42 when filming commenced in July 1988. The movie hit theaters in July 1989, by which time he was 43. Dalton almost played Bond again in 1995's "GoldenEye," but the film took some time to come together and when it did, former Bond custodians EON Productions had found someone new.

After Timothy Dalton's brief James Bond tenure came to an end, EON tapped a dashing young Irishman by the name of Pierce Brosnan to be his successor. 1995's "GoldenEye" is a pretty silly movie viewed in retrospect, but it will remain forever legendary for capturing the imagination of a whole new generation of Bond fans, who quickly became further enraptured by the video game tie-in.

Brosnan was born May 16, 1953, making him 41 when "GoldenEye" filming began in January 1995. The film bowed in theaters in November of that year, by which time he had turned 42 — just a year younger than Dalton in his final Bond performance.

Seven years later, Brosnan made his fourth and final appearance as 007 in "Die Another Day," which makes "GoldenEye" look like a work of pure artistic genius in comparison. Brosnan's now infamous final turn as 007 (it's the worst Bond film according to IMDb) started shooting in January 2002, at which point the actor was 48. When it hit theaters in November of that year he'd turned 49 and was well and truly done with the Bond franchise.

Daniel Craig will always be in contention for the title of best James Bond simply because he starred in the best James Bond movie ever made: 2006's "Casino Royale." Craig was born on March 2, 1968, and was 37 when filming began in January of 2006. That makes him the third youngest Bond to be cast in the role. He was 38 when "Casino Royale" arrived in theaters in November 2006.

Sadly, Craig's Bond tenure was characterized by diminishing returns and things went badly awry with 2021's "No Time to Die." Craig had clearly had enough by that point, too. The actor was 51 when filming started in April 2019, and 53 when the film was released in October 2021. It marked his fifth and final time playing Bond, and saw him become the second-oldest actor to ever portray the character after Roger Moore.

So, we come to the man himself. Robert Pattinson is now officially set to debut as James Bond in Denis Villeneuve's upcoming film. Just what the director has planned remains a mystery at this point, but casting Pattinson is a great start.

The actor beat out other finalists including Josh O'Connor, Jack Lowden, and Nicholas Hoult, to take the coveted role as England's greatest spy. Interestingly enough, he was the oldest of the bunch. The British actor was born on May 13 1986, making him 40 years old at the time he was cast as 007. The movie will likely start shooting in early 2027, so he will either be 40 or 41 at the time of filming. That puts Pattinson in the middle of the pack in terms of every Bond actor's age at the time of their casting.

Bond fans have reacted to Pattinson's casting with a mix of excitement and trepidation at what many see as a fairly safe choice. Those who've been following his career, however, should have no doubt he'll deliver in his Bond debut.

#3470. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.
