#3448. Why Casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond Is a High-Risk, High-Reward Gamble for Denis Villeneuve

Throughout his 64 years in movies, James Bond, the hard-living superspy, has been the star of the 007 franchise. But by granting Robert Pattinson a license to kill, the producers of the next Bond film are making a bet that one of the most famous men on the planet can slide into a role shaped by the likes of Sean Connery, Daniel Craig, Roger Moore, and Pierce Brosnan without bringing any Edward Cullen-sized baggage.

It’s quite a gamble. After all, Connery, Craig, Timothy Dalton, and poor, delusional George Lazenby were relative unknowns when they were tapped to play the secret agent, and Brosnan and Moore were TV-famous but unproven as film stars. That’s not the case with Pattinson, who has been one of the most recognizable people on the planet for two decades, and who is currently anchoring another massive franchise in “Batman.” So why did director Denis Villeneuve, producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal, and Amazon MGM Studios decide to hand over the keys to the Aston Martin to such a prominent and expensive candidate? Related Stories ’14th’ Trailer: Ava DuVernay Unpacks the Necessity of Another Essential Constitutional Amendment Robert Pattinson Is the Next James Bond: Denis Villeneuve Finds Star for His 007 Movie

Well, some of it has to do with Villeneuve’s comfort level. He’s worked with Pattinson on “Dune: Part Three” and knows what the mercurial star can bring to a role. Clearly, he wants to build a darker, brooding Bond. Then, there’s also the need to have insurance. Amazon is launching a new iteration of 007 into a world that looks very different than it did in 2019 when the last chapter, “No Time to Die,” was conceived and shot (it wouldn’t be released until 2021 thanks to COVID). We’ve lived through #MeToo, a pandemic, wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the fraying of the Western World and, with it, the “special relationship” Bond has sworn to protect. From the start, Amazon was interested in picking a higher-profile actor to outfit in one of Bond’s signature tuxedos. Before the search began in earnest last May, executives were high on the idea of Jacob Elordi.

Plus, some of the other finalists, a group that included Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, and Nicholas Hoult, lacked the kind of sex appeal and danger that the part required. Hoult apparently impressed executives with his audition, but came up short, as he did when he was in contention for Batman (losing out to Pattinson) and Superman (getting Lex Luthor as a consolation prize). He remains very well liked in the industry. With a salary estimated at roughly $2.5 million, Hoult would have been a cheaper option than Pattinson, who one industry source speculated would cost north of $10 million to hire.

But the higher price tag may be worth it. This isn’t just the first Bond to be released under Amazon’s ownership — it’s the first to be produced without the Broccoli family at the helm. The keepers of the 007 flame sold their creative control to Amazon in 2025, leaving the series without a guiding force. Both Heyman and Pascal are old hands, having overseen the casting of the Harry Potter and Spider-Man franchises, respectively, but those are still big shoes to fill.

What’s in it for Pattinson? Well, a chance to put his stamp on an iconic role, as well as an opportunity to reunite with Villeneuve, one of the hottest directors in Hollywood. His commercial bona fides have also, arguably, never been higher. Not only has he shown he can anchor a superhero film with “The Batman” and its upcoming sequel, but he’s also opened more idiosyncratic fare, such as the recent A24 hits “The Drama” and “Primetime.” Clearly, he can bring in the younger audiences driving the box office turnaround while retaining a kind of indie cool that could take Bond in a new and exciting direction. Will he be our perviest 007?

Plus, the recent shake-up at DC Studios, with James Gunn and Peter Safran replaced by former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham, may spell trouble for Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” series. Although it was conceived as a trilogy, the sequel was delayed multiple times as Reeves dealt with personal matters, forcing him to leave production last month, with Steven Soderbergh stepping in to finish shooting. DC may not want to wait as long to make another installment, and there’s a sense that Latcham may want something brighter and more mainstream than Reeves’ moody, hard PG-13 take on The Dark Knight.

But Pattinson better get ready for a lot more scrutiny than the questions that greeted his casting as Bruce Wayne. “With Batman, there’s a mask to hide behind,” said one industry source. “With Bond, your face is front and center.”

Even Craig, widely considered to be the best Bond since Connery, faced fierce blowback when his casting was announced. He was too blonde, too unconventionally handsome. A website, CraigNotBond, sprang up where fans vented their displeasure.

But when “Casino Royale” debuted in 2006, and Craig showed that he was perfectly capable of kicking ass and ordering his martini shaken, not stirred, the haters were quickly silenced. Will Pattinson be able to pull off the same stunt? It’s a high-risk, high-reward gamble. Just the kind of bet James Bond lives to make.

#3446. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

#3445. The Stop-Motion Tool That’s a Constant in This Crazy, AI-Mixed-Up World

A lot is happening in front of the camera in “Wildwood” — the general Millennial chaos of Portland, Oregon, swarms of baby-napping crows, an army of wolves with cannons and trebuchets — and just as much behind the camera in Laika Studios’ latest stop-motion epic. But for all the innovation and blending of CG and stop-motion required to tell the story of Prue McKeel’s (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) impossible quest into the impassable woods, some key tools have stayed the same for Laika since “Coraline.”

One such tool is Dragonframe, the frame-grabbing software developed by Jamie and Dyami Caliri in 2008, and essential to helping Laika animators craft the naturalistic performances that “Wildwood” director Travis Knight wanted to create. Related Stories Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber Why Casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond Is a High-Risk, High-Reward Gamble for Denis Villeneuve

“Back in the old days, like the Ray Harryhausen days — it was still the same as how we do it: You have a puppet; you have an object; you move it a tiny bit; you take a picture; you move it a little more; you take another picture. But you had no way of knowing exactly what the frame that you just took looked like and how it related to the frame that you’re about to take,” Knight explained on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “You had these gauges where you could try to approximate the distance something moved, but it was this act of faith. You didn’t really know; you had to wait until you developed the film to see how it moved. And that’s why a lot of early animation has that kind of herky-jerky quality.”

Dragonframe and other frame-grabbing software systems take a lot of the guesswork, if not quite all of the faith, out of that process. Laika animators can check what they’ve just done on a computer, moving between the most recent frames taken and the one that an animator is currently on. This allows animators to ensure that whatever motion they’re puppeting, be it walking, running, flying, or the unfathomable wrath of nature flowing out through a giant tower of living vines exploding forth from the Earth, flows together.

“Whether it’s a 20-frame shot or a 1000-frame shot, you can look at all the frames that precede it to make sure that the object or the puppet is moving the way it should,” Knight told IndieWire.

Laika has used Dragonframe on every one of its films, but just because a tool is that useful and reliable doesn’t take the artistry and effort of animating out of the equation, or lower the particular stakes of stop-motion.

“2D animation, CG animation, they’re iterative. You can set key frames. You do your breakdowns. You do your in-betweens. You can go back and refine and keep going and reworking things until you get the perfect performance. With stop-motion, it’s progressive. You start on frame one, and the animator, coaxing life with their hands into this puppet, is working their way through a frame at a time. You don’t get to go back and change it.”

That lack of take-backs permanence, though, also helps stop-motion animators be intentional and certain in their choices. “You’re contorting your body into all these positions to get these puppets to move properly. It’s mentally very draining because you have to do all this three-dimensional chess as you’re trying to figure things out, because it is technical, but it always has to feel organic,” Knight said. “ It’s human ingenuity, it’s human creativity, it’s devotion, it’s care, it’s time.”

All that care and time goes into pulling off the magic trick of making steel, silicon, and fabric objects feel fully alive. That’s been the game for stop-motion since Ray Harryhausen. Whenever Laika develops new processes or sticks with tried-and-true tools, it’s to give animators the ability to do that. “[We don’t want] to get in the way of seeing this puppet as a person. The finest stop-motion animators can do all that with their hands. But we’ve developed different techniques and tools where some of the less experienced animators can actually get to that same level,” Knight said.

#3444. Best Isekai Books Like Dungeon Crawler Carl

Dungeon Crawler Carl by Matt Dinniman is not, technically, an isekai. The genre was popularized in Japan, and in the genre's current form, it centers around an ordinary person who's suddenly transported or reborn into another world. Carl isn't relocated to a different world—the madness comes to his world. But it does have all the other makings of an isekai: an ordinary dude has to go up against RPG-like elements such as monsters, leveling up, loot, questing, and so on.

Of course, there are plenty of litRPG books for fans of DCC, but there are also plenty of isekai that fans of Dinniman's books would enjoy. Lots of manga and anime play off the "adventuring in another world" trope, but we'll take a look at the light novels, specifically, which are breezy, fast-paced and fun to read bite-sized novels that are designed to be portable.

Grab one (or all) of these recommendations, because you never know when you might need some light reading when you're out and about on your own epic adventures... or just commuting to work. Plus, quite a few of these have accompanying anime, so you can continue the journey off the page, too!

In So I'm A Spider, So What? (available for purchase here) a freak accident causes an entire Japanese high school to be obliterated and killed. Most are reincarnated into another world as nobles, adventurers, and other characters. But one girl is reincarnated in a dungeon as the lowest and weakest monster of them all: a tiny spider.

Of course, part of the fun of an isekai is watching the underdog go from nothing to being kind of a big deal in the world, just like in Dungeon Crawler Carl. Over her adventures, the spider grows more and more powerful, makes some very useful allies (and, of course, some dangerous enemies), and becomes an influential figure in this strange new world.

The protagonist of Completionist Chronicles (available for purchase here) is an ordinary Joe, literally. Unlike in a traditional isekai, Joe doesn't get run over by a truck or die to get reborn. Instead, he makes a choice to permanently start over his life inside a game.

As soon as he does, Joe realizes that he has some abilities that make him a wanted man in the world. Forced to practice his forbidden magic in secret, he makes it his mission to learn more about the world. Joe won't settle for just a slight glimpse of the game; he's after that 100% completion achievement. He's going to get every item, skill, ability, and every bit of knowledge that this world has to offer, or die trying.

The Rising Of The Shield Hero (available here) follows Naofumi, just an ordinary nerdy guy who's suddenly summoned to another universe. He learns that he's one of the four legendary heroes who are destined to save the world from destruction. Unfortunately, he's the weakest and least impressive of them all: the Shield Hero.

Without a powerful weapon, Naofumi has to rely on his brains, strategies, and loyal allies who he meets along the way. Together, they fight monsters, unravel political plots, and find a way to rise above his weak-seeming shield and do his part to save this fantasy world he's found himself in.

In Dungeon Crawler Carl, Carl's survival depends largely on his use of, essentially, a hidden tool. That's also the case for Solo Leveling (available for purchase here). This series is also technically not an isekai, since Jinwoo Sung isn't transported to another world permanently. Instead, mysterious Gates suddenly appear in his world, which connect to other worlds full of dangerous monsters.

In Jinwoo's world, some people "awaken" to become fighters while others stay as weak non-fighters. Jinwoo is one of the latter. The thing is, once you awaken, you're assigned a rank, and you stay at that rank forever. One day, Jinwoo finds that he can do something no one else can: he can level up.

This changes everything. As the only person in the world who can level up and increase his strength, Jinwoo grows in power by fighting through dungeons. As he does, he uncovers the secrets of these Gates and what's happening in his world.

The idea behind Log Horizon (available for purchase here) is based around an MMORPG—a massively multiplayer online role-playing game. One day, 30,000 players wake up to find themselves trapped inside their beloved multiplayer video game, Elder Tales. The game becomes much more serious when they realize that they might be stuck in this digital world forever, with no way to escape.

A group of adventurers bands together to find a way back to their home world. They travel around the fantasy world, defeat monsters, and search for clues about what's happening. And soon, they discover something even more alarming: They respawn after death, but lose a little more of their memories each time. The fight to survive and return home begins now!

With two such similar genres as litRPG and isekai, there's bound to be some overlap. He Who Fights with Monsters (available for purchase here) sits right at that intersection between the Western litRPG and Japanese isekai.

Jason is just your run-of-the-mill office supplies middle manager until he's transported to another world. On his very first day, he has to fend against monsters, wizards, cultists, and cannibals. Like Carl, Jason has to use his wits and some special powers to stay alive in this wild world. The only problem is that he's a pretty decent guy, but all his powers are evil.

In DCC, Carl's cat Princess Donut captures the spotlight. The young cat girl in Reincarnated as as Sword (available for purchase here) is also at the center of the story, but as the title suggests, she's not the main character here.

Instead, the protagonist is an office worker who's reincarnated in the fantast world as a sentient sword. He remembers his old life, but not his name, so he becomes the girl's Teacher in both name and status. They work together to achieve both their goals: She wants to become stronger, and he wants to know why he's in this world. They learn more about themselves, too, and become an unstoppable team.

In That Time I Got Reincarnated As A Slime (available for purchase here), a guy stuck at a dead-end job meets his untimely end at the hands of a robber. As he's dying, he unknowingly makes a pact with a strange system that resurrects him in another world... as a slime, of course.

Like the spider from So I'm a Spider, So What?, the little slime doesn't stay weak for very long. He uses his special connection with the aforementioned system to acquire some extremely useful skills, then heads out on his adventure.

As the slime meets new characters, he uses his strategic way of thinking to forge some extremely powerful alliances. Just like Dungeon Crawler Carl, the slime's story revolves around a fight for survival and acquiring power. And just like DCC, the slime gets more and more involved in the overall lore and politics of the world, sending him on more epic adventures each time.

#3442. ‘The Rings of Power’ Just Dropped a Direct Callback to Peter Jackson’s Trilogy in 3 Minutes

Julio is a Senior Author for Collider. He studied History and International Relations at university, but found his calling in cultural journalism. When he isn't writing, Julio also teaches English at a nearby school. He has lived in São Paulo most of his life, where he covers CCXP and other big events. Having loved movies, music, and TV from an early age, he prides himself in knowing every minute detail about the things he loves. When he is older, he dreams of owning a movie theater in a small countryside town.

Editor's note: The below contains spoilers for The Rings of Power Season 3.

It's been a long wait, but The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is finally back, bigger and better, with Season 3. There are many great storylines in the four-episode premiere, although none as interesting as the journey Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova), and Marnûkh (Adam Young) embark on toward the fortress of Gundabad in the North. The unlikely trio faces many dangers along the way, chief among them a close encounter in Episode 3, "The Secret Fire," in a scene that is a direct callback to an iconic (and terrifying) moment in Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring.

The Rings of Power's introduction of the Nazgnagôl is one of Season 3's most compelling elements; they are technically an early version of the Nazgûl since the One Ring hasn't been forged yet, and they still haven't been consumed by its will. They are already fearsome and powerful, though, and have sharp tracking skills, as they nearly catch Galadriel, Arondir, and Marnûkh in a clearing in the woods just as they almost catch Frodo (Elijah Wood), Sam (Sean Astin), Merry (Dominic Monaghan), and Pippin (Billy Boyd) in the Shire millennia later in The Fellowship of the Ring.

Both scenes align almost perfectly, with clear visual and narrative callbacks, from the Black Riders' sudden arrival to how the heroes manage to sneak out. Galadriel is warned of their presence by her own ring of power, just as Frodo feels it through the One Ring. In both, the heroes hide among the vegetation, with Arondir and Frodo coming dangerously close to revealing their locations and being stopped by Galadriel and Sam, respectively. They eventually distract the Riders and are able to sneak out — Galadriel invokes a swarm of butterflies, and Merry throws a decoy bag to lead the Nazgûl away.

Córdova shares how personal loss and close on-set bonds shaped the culmination of Arondir's Season 3 storyline.

The obvious difference is that, in The Rings of Power, the moment features two Black Riders, while, in the movie, only one comes close to discovering the hiding Hobbits. This actually says much about who the Nazgnagôl are right now; they're still able to recognize and be swayed by beauty. The Nazgûl, meanwhile, feel nothing but the pull of the One Ring. But it shouldn't take much longer for the Nazgnagôl to get to that stage.

The Rings of Power Season 3's four-episode premiere has many such nods to J.R.R. Tolkien lore, but, curiously, the scene when Galadriel, Arondir, and Marnûkh hide from the Nazgnagôl in the clearing in the woods isn't one of them. That's because the equivalent moment in the movies doesn't originate from the source material. There is a similar moment in the books, but the concept of the Hobbits huddling under a tree root comes from Ralph Bakshi, with Jackson giving it his own spin in his movie trilogy.

Before The Lord of the Rings, Jackson was largely known for his work in horror, with movies like Braindead and The Frighteners becoming cult classics, and those origins clearly inform Fellowship of the Ring's Nazgûl scene. It's the proper introduction of the Black Riders, and one of the most chilling moments in the movie. Jackson keeps the monster from us for as long as possible, and raises the tension by focusing on Frodo and the Ring instead of the Nazgûl — with the Ring being a monster in itself, too, in a way.

The Rings of Power approaches its own Nazgnagôl moment the exact same way. We've just been introduced to the Black Riders, and they already show many mannerisms they will carry well into their existence as Nazgûl, too. Instead of tension, however, the focus is on showing how even simple things can always prevail over darkness, hence the shift to the butterfly and the following swarm.

One of the biggest changes in The Rings of Power Season 3 is the Harfoots' plot being cut, but there are still plenty of nods and references to the Hobbits besides the Nazgnagôl encounter in the clearing. In fact, Galadriel and Arondir's journey with Marnûkh directly echoes Frodo and Sam's journey with Gollum (Andy Serkis) in The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers and The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King in almost every way, including how the Orc tries to pit the two Elves against each other.

The culmination of the story in The Rings of Power, however, is much more tragic, including the deaths of two of the three members of this strange company. Sad as that outcome is, the scene in the clearing is this brief fellowship's finest hour, with all of them working together in some capacity to evade the Black Riders.

#3441. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.

#3440. Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber

This year’s TIFF and Venice were quieter in terms of breakout sales, especially when compared to last year’s splash for “Obsession,” and several awards contenders were scooped up before they even premiered at the festival. But other smaller buyers have emerged in recent weeks to release some of the more critically acclaimed titles that didn’t land major sales ahead of time.

The festivals are long done, but we’re still tracking every sale that happens, so check back frequently.

Distributor: Kino LorberDirector: Maiken BairdFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: This documentary about Palestinian-American author and intellectual Edward Said earned strong reaction in its premiere at TIFF and festivals like NYFF and IDFA, in part because though he’s been dead for over 20 years, his writing and his views have been far more relevant in a post-October 7 landscape. IndieWire’s review out of TIFF praised the construction of the documentary and how it manages to be decades-spanning and comprehensive in a manageable running time. And Anne Thompson spoke with the filmmakers about the challenges of making the documentary and the fear that it being about Palestine would pose barriers to a distributor stepping up to buy it. Thankfully, Kino Lorber did just that, and it will be planning a theatrical release for 2027. Distributor: Cohen Media GroupDirector: May el-ToukhyFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: Venice’s top prize winner of the Golden Lion has found a U.S. deal, this one made out of AFM with Cohen Media Group. The Danish film, also Denmark’s official Oscar selection, is a period drama set after World War II about a former housekeeper now set to be married to the household’s wealthy patriarch. Distributor: Sony Pictures ClassicsDirector: Niki ByrneFestival: TIFF Special PresentationsBuzz: Sony Pictures Classics have acquired all rights in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore) to “The Julia Set,” written and directed by Niki Byrne. The film had its world premiere at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival and follows a gifted young math prodigy (“One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti) who is “recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics, while at the same time falling into a romantic relationship with her charismatic teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney).”

Distributor: Strand ReleasingDirector: Hanaël El YousfiFestival: TIFF DiscoveryBuzz: This directorial debut follows two friends, one Muslim and one Jewish, spending a carefree summer in Marseille, only to see the expectations and tensions between their traditional families start to get in the way of their friendship and leads them to take hold of their own destinies. #3439. Ex-Transportation Secretary Says Air Traffic Control System Needs To Fix One Tower At A Time

Ray LaHood -- the former Secretary of Transportation -- says people should expect more ground stops, delays, and screw-ups with air travel in the future ... because it's painstaking to update one of the world's most antiquated air traffic control systems.

Ray -- who served during President Barack Obama's first term -- joined us on "TMZ Live" Monday ... and he heaped praise on the professional Air Traffic Controllers who keep fliers safe ... especially because they're usually doing it on an ancient system.

That said, Ray warns the system itself ain't up to snuff ... and it's not like the United States government can just flip a switch and magically update the whole darn thing.

Basically, Ray says they have to go from air traffic control tower to another, updating each location ... which is slow and painstaking work.

Ray also gets into the dollars and cents of the whole situation ... explaining that his administration updated the infrastructure with $5 billion -- though he understands that the $50 billion current Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is asking for will make the work go faster.

As for why Duffy upped the number to $50 billion from $30 billion, Ray says it's all part of the Washington, D.C., dance ... ask for more than you need and maybe get what you want.

We're keeping our fingers crossed for smooth flights in the future ... and Ray is, too!

#3438. 8 War Movie Masterpieces Praised By Real-Life Veterans

War movies movies have been a consistent genre throughout the history of cinema. Hollywood has repeatedly tapped into the stories of real-life conflicts, showing dramatized versions of what really happened. These efforts came with great rewards, too, as countless war movies have been hugely successful at the worldwide box office.

Audiences typically look for a lot of things when choosing their next war movie to watch — action, drama between characters, and potentially world-defining stakes. Yet, there’s another element that typically comes into play, too, and that is what real-life veterans think of a given film. After all, getting their stamp of approval is mightily important to any war movie, as it shows that the story they told is (for the most part) accurate to what really happened.

Some war movies have been praised for their portrayal of the conflict at hand. Andrew Garfield’s Hacksaw Ridge, which tells the story of a soldier who, due to his strong religious beliefs, opts not to carry a weapon of any kind during battle, is one war film that has been praised repeatedly. These accolades have come not only from historians who have spent their entire careers studying the conflict, but veterans who were actually there, too.

War films praised by veterans aren’t just limited to World War II, either. Movies that have centered on more recent conflicts, such as the wars in the Middle East, have also been lauded by those who served for their accuracy of their portrayal of history. Regardless, war movies remain an incredibly popular subgenre in Hollywood today, and if they’re praised by real-life veterans, then chances go up that it’s an excellent film as well.

Andrew Garfield’s Hacksaw Ridge is one war movie that has consistently been praised by real-life veterans. As stated, the film tells the story of Desmond Doss, a Seventh-Day Adventist who objected to conflict of any kind. However, when drafted into the United States military, he was forced to either forgo his religion or risk criminal punishment for not fighting.

Miraculously, Doss found a solution to this problem — not carrying a weapon at all. During combat, such as at the Battle of Okinawa (he later received a Medal of Honor for his actions during the battle), Doss had no weapons on him. He had no rifle, no pistol, and nothing that could cause harm to another human being, as Doss was adamant that he wouldn’t hurt anyone. Instead, he served as a medic, thus saving the lives of those on the battlefield, and earning a reputation as one of the bravest soldiers in history in the process.

When Hacksaw Ridge released in theaters in 2016, the question naturally arose about how much of the film’s story was accurate to real events. After all, while some war movies are based in realism, others also take plenty of story liberties. Garfield’s Hacksaw Ridge wasn’t one of these films, however, and has instead been praised by several veterans.

For example, the film’s director, Mel Gibson, showed the finished product at the Disabled American Veterans national convention in Atlanta, Georgia. The film received great applause upon its conclusion, with many veterans praising its accuracy. Dan Clare, an Iraqi war veteran, noted that Hacksaw Ridge was a surprise hit with the crowd.

“These were people who avoid war movies because they fear they will either be unrealistic or that they will trigger post-traumatic stress. To their surprise, most people felt that it was a realistic depiction of combat — one of the most accurate ever — and, by and large, they appreciated the way it portrayed PTSD. Bottom line? Unlike most Hollywood movies, this one felt like it represented us.”

Ridley Scott’s 2001 film Black Hawk Down tells the story of two Black Hawk helicopters that were shot down during the Battle of Mogadishu. Once again, this film was praised for its depiction of the battle that its based on, with many veterans who fought during this conflict noting the film’s accuracy. Not only that, but one veteran stated that “90–95% of the film” is accurate, a high number that shows just how much attention to detail went into this movie.

Another more recent title, The Outpost is based on a non-fiction book by newscaster Jake Tapper. The film tells the story of the Battle of Kamdesh and the United States soldiers stationed at the Combat Outpost (COP) Keating in Afghanistan. A fatal design flaw of the base meant that the soldiers were vulnerable to ambush from the surrounding mountains, and the film then shows their desperate fight to survive.

One of the things that makes The Outpost such a unique film is that it not only received praise from veterans, but was actually worked on by veterans, too. Director Rod Lurie is a graduate of West Point and served in the U.S. Army, and not only that, but the film also recruited several survivors from the actual events to serve as advisers on the story. This helps to make The Outpost feel raw, lived in, and true to real-life events.

Another recent film with plenty of veteran involvement is Warfare, which tells the story of an encounter that a group of Marines had shortly after the Battle of Ramadi in 2006. Interestingly, the film is told in real time, with each second passing at the same rate for both the audience and the characters. Not only that, but the script was also based solely on personal accounts that survivors gave after the attack occurred.

These methods were praised by veterans, including survivors, for adding to the film’s overall authenticity. In particular, veterans praised the “smaller moments” for depicting the quiet moments of battle, which many war films skip over. The performances of the cast were also praised, as actors like Joseph Quinn and Will Poulter did extensive research to make their portrayals as accurate as possible.

One of the earliest films on this list is The Best Years of Our Lives, which released just one year after the conclusion of World War II, in 1946. The film tells the story of three United States soldiers who return to their small towns after serving, but find the transition back to civilian life especially difficult. For example, Al Stephenson (played by Frederic March) struggles with alcoholism upon his return and, at the same time, also has a very difficult job at a bank, in which he is given the task of approving or denying loans for fellow veterans.

The Best Years of Our Lives is timeless in this regard. The film may focus on World War II veterans, but it can just as easily translate to virtually every conflict in modern human history, with soldiers struggling to find their footing after returning home. The realistic-ness of this portrayal was praised by veterans upon its release, many of whom felt seen by the film. Amazingly, many of the film’s actors were veterans themselves, including Harold Russell, who, just like his character, lost both his hands during the war.

The head of Veterans Affairs at the time, General Omar Bradley, praised this film upon its release. In fact, he was such a fan of the movie that he organized a showing for VA headquarters staff, and later went on to write to the film’s producer to express his appreciation.

Steven Spielberg has directed so many iconic films in his career, and Saving Private Ryan is right up there among the very best. The film, which released in 1998, tells the story of a battalion of U.S. soldiers who set out on a mission to rescue Private James Francis Ryan (after his brothers had already tragically been lost in battle). Tom Hanks plays Captain John Miller, the leader of the rescue mission, and Matt Damon takes on the role of Private Ryan.

Many World War II veterans, some of whom actually fought in the specific battles that Saving Private Ryan depicts, praised Spielberg’s film. D-Day veterans noted that the Omaha Beach sequence captured the true violence of the war, with paratrooper Jack Evans saying: “A lot of people will see this and think it's gruesome, but that's the way it was. There were a lot of times it was a lot worse."

One of the most recent films on this list, Atonement tells the true story of a deadly battle during the Iraq War and its longstanding aftermath. Starring Kenneth Branagh and Boyd Holbrook, Atonement begins with an extended sequence showing American soldiers patrolling the streets of a populated Iraqi village. They hear gunfire, however, and this quickly sends them into action.

On the civilian side of things, an Iraqi family similarly hears the gunfire and decides to make a run for it and escape to their hometown. What happens, though, ends up being a tragedy in every sense of the word, as the family is caught in the crossfire between Iraqi militants and the U.S. Army. Their attempts to inform the latter that they aren’t a threat prove to be fatal, however, as several of the family members are killed by U.S. soldiers, who mistakenly think of them as a threat.

Atonement is based directly not just on real events, but on real people, too. The Khachaturian family were the ones impacted by this tragedy, and Boyd Holbrook’s Lou D'Alessandro was (one of) the real soldiers in question. Meanwhile, Kenneth Branagh’s Michael Reid was the journalist who covered the events (and who facilitated a meeting between both parties years later).

When the film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in September, director Reed Van Dyk stated that he wanted to honor those in this story by depicting the events as accurately as possible. During the Q&A after the film’s premiere, Van Dyk noted that he and his team had received the stamp of approval from veterans who served during the War in Iraq, with particular praise going to the intensity of the combat sequence that then sets up the rest of the movie.

The 1993 film Gettysburg tells the story of the Battle of Gettysburg during the American Civil War in the mid-1800s. The film, which is written and directed by Ronald F. Maxwell, was originally filmed as a miniseries but was released for a limited run in theaters after positive reception. Because of this, it remains the longest film released in theaters in U.S. history.

Because of how long ago this war was, no direct veterans were around to see this movie. However, veterans of future conflicts noted that Gettysburg has a surprising commitment to depicting all aspects of war. Not only that, but historians praised Maxwell for including real battlefield formations, re-enactors, and for filming near the real locations where key battles took place.

#3435. Robert Pattinson as James Bond Proves That IP Is No Longer the New Movie Stars

Every James Bond casting announcement marks the start of a new era. The fictional MI6 agent has been one of pop culture’s few constants over the past seven decades; and each time a new actor steps into the role, it tells us something about the entertainment landscape we currently inhabit. Bonds can be intensely serious or silly and self-deprecating, and actors have entered the franchise at ages ranging from their late twenties to mid-forties. The role always goes to a member of the Commonwealth, but the variation that’s possible within those parameters has turned the franchise into a vertical wine tasting that illustrates what male movie stardom looks like in each decade. Related Stories Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber The Stop-Motion Tool That’s a Constant in This Crazy, AI-Mixed-Up World

The first Bond of the Amazon MGM era was destined to be even more of a turning point than usual, no matter who landed the role. The next film in the franchise will be the first one ever produced without the involvement of the Broccoli family, who have carefully guarded each iteration of the character since “Dr. No” came out in 1962. It marks the biggest movie investment that Amazon has ever made, as the tech giant spent nearly $10 billion to acquire MGM (of which Bond was the clear crown jewel) and then wrestle full control away from the Broccolis.

With Denis Villeneuve at the helm, it arguably marks the first time that Bond has been rebooted by a true auteur director with a distinct preexisting style and fan base. And it follows a Daniel Craig era that many feel took the idea of a dark, realistic James Bond to its logical endpoint with no obvious direction to go next.

When Robert Pattinson was officially announced as the seventh actor to play 007 on Monday morning, the latest era of the Bond franchise officially took shape. But it also marked the end of a larger Hollywood era in which blue chip legacy characters were seen as infinitely more important than the people playing them. We spent much of the past decade declaring that intellectual property is the new movie star(s). But casting the current Batman actor as James Bond proves that is no longer the case.

That line of thinking began to take shape in the 2010s, an era of Hollywood that will forever be defined by the phrase “cinematic universe.” As moviegoing became less of a consistent consumer habit and more of an event-driven hobby, the industry found that putting an A-list movie star or two in a new film was no longer enough to guarantee a big opening weekend. What did work, though, was slapping a Marvel logo in front of something and watching the box office dollars flow in.

Top-tier franchises were places where you went to build your star power, not cash it in. A new Bond or Spider-Man announcement was often the mainstream world’s introduction to a rising star that would be a household name within a few years. The approach was certainly better for the producers who steward these franchises: it ensured that the real value was contained in the stories and iconography that they controlled, making it relatively easy to bring in massive box office hauls with interchangeable actors who often moved onto bigger things before they became too expensive or demanding.

As that formula becomes less workable, it’s fair to wonder where we’ll start going to find our new stars. If you were casting a new Spider-Man in this environment, you probably wouldn’t pick an obscure theater actor like Tom Holland. We’re already seeing more stars come out of independent genre films, one of the few niches that can still be profitable without star power. “Obsession” gave the world its biggest breakout star of 2026 in Inde Navarette, and now she’s heading to the Marvel Cinematic Universe to help lead the “X-Men” franchise. But legacy franchises were once Hollywood’s most reliable path to minting new stars, and the industry will have to get creative if it doesn’t want the pipeline of bankable stars to fizzle out.

From an artistic standpoint, there’s every reason to believe Pattinson will make an excellent Bond. He has already worked with Villeneuve on the upcoming “Dune: Part Three” and has proven himself to be one of his generation’s most versatile leading men. He’s equally capable of playing brooding heroes and sniveling villains; a 2026 slate that includes “The Drama,” “The Odyssey,” and “Primetime” is evidence of both his range and consistent box office appeal. But from a business standpoint, it’s a decision that you wouldn’t make if you didn’t have to.

His deal reportedly costs more money for less commitment than any of the other finalists who screen tested. You’ll be juggling a production and promotion schedule that also includes “The Batman” franchise and other major films. In the run-up to the movie, more eyes will be on the man himself than the timelessness of the brand. And when the time eventually comes to replace him, expectations for the level of actor you need to land will be higher than ever before. It’s the kind of move you make when you simply cannot afford to fail. Nobody would deny that that’s the exact situation Amazon MGM finds itself in, but the mere fact that something as reliable as a new James Bond movie could place a studio in such a position is notable in and of itself.

It would be reductive to say that the pendulum has entirely swung back towards favoring movie stars. The old model where you could regularly deliver hits by putting George Clooney and Julia Roberts on a poster is certainly nowhere to be found. It might be more accurate to say that we’re in a “more is more” era of Hollywood, where no film is ever guaranteed to become the kind of cultural event that’s required to turn a profit on these massive tentpole budgets. With more competition for audience attention spans than ever before, you need to pair the power of Bond and the power of Pattinson and Villeneuve to feel truly comfortable with your investment.

#3433. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.

#3431. Cary Grant, Clint Eastwood, and Christian Bale: The Stars Who Almost Played James Bond

When director Denis Villeneuve selected Robert Pattinson to play secret agent 007 in the next James Bond movie, he broke with tradition by casting an undeniable movie star in the role. Earlier Bonds were either relatively unknown (Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Daniel Craig, Timothy Dalton) or big names in television who hadn’t yet proven themselves on the big screen (Roger Moore, Pierce Brosnan). Yet Villeneuve and producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal’s choice of Pattinson isn’t completely at odds with the franchise’s history. At several points in the last 64 years, some of the box office’s biggest draws have flirted with the role and either turned it down or been rejected by the filmmakers. Related Stories Robert Pattinson as James Bond Proves That IP Is No Longer the New Movie Stars Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber

Right from the beginning, Bond producers were torn between going after a bankable name and letting the character be the star. Cary Grant was one of the world’s most famous actors when producers Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and Harry Saltzman began pre-production on “Dr. No,” the first feature film to showcase James Bond. (The character had previously been played by “The Shining” hotel manager Barry Nelson in a 1954 TV adaptation of “Casino Royale.”) He was also a close friend of Broccoli’s — so close, in fact, that he was best man at the Broccoli’s wedding.

Alas, that personal relationship wasn’t enough to get Grant to play Bond as Broccoli wanted. Grant was already starting to wind down his career and wanted to leave the public with their impression of him as a dashing young man. By 1966, he was done, so signing a multi-picture contract to star as Bond in 1962 didn’t appeal to the soon-to-be retired actor. Broccoli and Saltzman’s requirement that their Bond sign a long-term contract was also an obstacle for two other famous actors they approached. Both James Mason and Peter Lawford bristled at the idea of being committed to Bond for three or more films.

Rex Harrison and David Niven both wanted the part but were turned down in favor of Sean Connery, whose most prominent role to date was in the Disney movie “Darby O’Gill and the Little People.” “Dr. No” and its sequels made Connery a star, and for many viewers he remains the definitive Bond. By the time the sixth 007 movie, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” rolled around in 1969, however, Connery was tired of the role and stepped away — launching the first major search for a new James Bond.

Given that Connery wasn’t a household name when he made Bond an international icon in “Dr. No,” Broccoli and Saltzman were less inclined to go after a major movie star than they had been during the James Mason and Cary Grant discussions; most of the people seriously considered for “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” weren’t particularly popular at the time, and are even less well known now. (Few modern movie buffs would be able to pick John Richardson or Anthony Rogers out of a lineup, though the more famous Terence Stamp did meet with Broccoli about the role.)

The most popular actor Broccoli and Saltzman pursued was “Batman” star Adam West, who turned the part down because he felt 007 should be British — a response that would be repeated by other actors the next time a new Bond was needed, which turned out to be a lot sooner than Broccoli or Saltzman would have liked. Male model George Lazenby had almost zero acting experience when he secured the coveted role, but he took his good fortune for granted. In one of the great cinematic miscalculations in history, he assumed James Bond’s days were numbered in the age of “Easy Rider,” and declined to return for more 007 adventures.

Back at square one, Broccoli and Saltman decided to reverse course and once again go after big movie stars, including American ones. They offered “Diamonds Are Forever” to Clint Eastwood, who, like West, turned down the role because he felt Bond should be British. He would, however, direct and star in his own Bond-esque spy adventure, “The Eiger Sanction,” a few years later. Burt Reynolds, as famous for the hits he turned down (“Die Hard,” “Pretty Woman”) as for the ones he made, turned down Bond for the same reason.

John Gavin, best known today for his roles in Alfred Hitchcock’s “Psycho” and Douglas Sirk’s “Imitation of Life,” had no such reservations about playing Bond, and was the first American cast in the role. Unfortunately for him, Connery had second thoughts and decided to come back one last time, so Gavin was out, and Connery was in for “Diamonds Are Forever.” Gavin was briefly considered again for the eighth Bond picture, “Live and Let Die,” but by then the producers decided 007 should, in fact, be British and went with television star Roger Moore.

Moore had actually been offered “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” but had to turn it down due to an episodic series commitment. He became one of the longest-running Bonds, starring in seven 007 movies between 1973 and 1985. However, he began grumbling about leaving the series as early as 1979, leading the filmmakers to open discussions with Timothy Dalton (who turned down the role in “For Your Eyes Only” before committing to the series with 1987’s “The Living Daylights”) and James Brolin, whose bags were packed to play what would have been (again) the first American Bond in “Octopussy” when Moore had a change of heart.

The tradition of actors who either turned down or missed out on Bond in earlier films coming back to play the character was a sturdy one: just as Moore and Dalton would play the character in multiple films after initial false starts, Pierce Brosnan lost out on “The Living Daylights” due to a scheduling conflict (with his series “Remington Steele”) before replacing Dalton in 1995’s “GoldenEye.” Before the producers committed to Dalton in “Living Daylights,” a wide range of actors were considered and approached. Brosnan was the frontrunner, but Sam Neill came close, and the studio wanted Mel Gibson, but Broccoli overruled it, once again wanting a Brit (never mind the near-casting of James Brolin).

Although Brosnan was perhaps inevitable as Dalton’s replacement given the producers’ thwarted desire to have him in the 1980s, Hugh Grant, Sean Bean, and Liam Neeson were all considered for “GoldenEye.” Neeson turned the part down, later admitting that his girlfriend (and eventual wife) Natasha Richardson didn’t want him to play it. The producers wanted Bean but were overruled by MGM. Luckily for the actor, he made a strong enough impression to score a role as the picture’s villain.

Brosnan would play Bond four times, from “GoldenEye” through 2002’s “Die Another Day.” After that, the producers decided to make a change (reportedly because Brosnan’s salary demands were getting too high) and reboot the franchise with “Casino Royale.” Several now noteworthy actors were considered before Daniel Craig snared the part and became (after a brief initial flurry of internet outrage) the franchise’s most beloved Bond since Connery; Clive Owen, Sam Worthington, and Matthew Rhys were all in the running, and Henry Cavill was high on director Martin Campbell’s list.

Most intriguingly, Christian Bale turned down the part, which producer Barbara Broccoli said was his for the asking after she saw his stunning turn in Mary Harron’s “American Psycho.” Bale, amusingly, said he didn’t want to play Bond since he had already just played “a serial killer.” He also, according to the book “Christian Bale: The Inside Story of the Darkest Batman,” felt the role played into “despicable” stereotypes. Bale’s loss was Craig’s gain, as he led the Bond franchise into one of its most artistically and commercially successful periods — leaving Robert Pattinson with sizable shoes to fill.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that you're less likely to see throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech.

#3429. Apple TV’s Masterpiece Spy Thriller Series Is So Good, It’s Renewed For 4 More Seasons

Apple TV's spy thriller series has scored an unprecedented win on streaming, with four more seasons confirmed to be on the way, and it just proves how the show is unmatched when it comes to the genre. The espionage genre has become the talk of the town lately, as all eyes turned to one of the biggest movie franchises of all time.

After all, Dune director Denis Villeneuve was charged with casting Daniel Craig's replacement as James Bond for the suave spy's new movie. After a long casting process with many rumors and conflicting reports, The Batman star Robert Pattinson has been officially announced to play James Bond. That reveal comes on the same day that one of Apple TV's best shows released its own exciting future update.

In a competitive streaming market where espionage thrillers have become some of the most popular shows around, Apple TV continues to thrive with a long-running British spy series. The show in question faces competition from hits like Michael Fassbender's The Agency, Gabriel Basso's The Night Agent, Richard Madden's Citadel, John Krasinski's Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan, and more genre successes.

However, only Slow Horses has managed to go the distance with six seasons so far, and all of them being released on an annual schedule. In fact, the first two seasons of Slow Horses arrived on Apple TV in the same year, 2022, showing how the spy thriller differs from its genre competition. Now, Slow Horses just got a massive future update that further sets it apart from other espionage TV shows.

The Slow Horses season 6 finale aired on October 21, but the show's future was already confirmed to extend well beyond its latest season. After all, Apple TV renewed Slow Horses for season 7 in July 2025, while the hit show was confirmed to come back for season 8 more recently, in September, right before Slow Horses season 6 was released on the streaming service. Based on the Mick Herron series of novels following the agents of Slough House, seasons 7 and 8 will be based on the books Bad Actors and Clown Town, respectively, but that is not all.

Slow Horses boasts a near-perfect 97% overall critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes for its six seasons.

Recently, Sid Baker actress Olivia Cooke, who returned to the show in season 6 after a prolonged absence, indicated that Slow Horses might call it a day after season 8. Talking to The Times, Cooke claimed she was shooting the final season of the Apple TV spy thriller series and that the show coming to an end was "what we’ve been told." However, the future could not be brighter for fans of the espionage drama, as Apple TV has officially confirmed that Slow Horses has been renewed for seasons 9 and 10. That said, it means a major change is happening.

So far, all seasons of Slow Horses have had source material to adapt, mostly covering a single book of Herron's fan-favorite series of novels. However, that franchise runs out of books to adapt with the upcoming release of season 8, which should happen in 2028, if the show keeps to its annual release schedule. While Herron has plans to write more books in the franchise, he has a tighter deadline now in place if they are to be adapted, with seasons 9 and 10 likely to begin filming soon, given how Slow Horses season 8 filming is underway two years before its release.

Besides running out of source material to adapt, Slow Horses seasons 9 and 10 could have had to deal with another major change, as the presence of Jack Lowden's River Cartwright was uncertain when the series' renewal was announced. After all, the actor was a finalist for the role of the next James Bond, and if he got the role, that likely meant Slow Horses losing River, a key part of the show throughout all seasons. However, with Robert Pattinson as the new 007, Lowden is expected to remain as Slow Horses works through its four upcoming seasons.

#3427. ‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Riveting Comeback Remakes Claude Chabrol and ‘Unfaithful’ for a Hopeless Wartime Russia

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 19, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release the film in theaters Friday, November 20.]

Andrey Zvyagintsev nearly died and then came back to life in 2021 amid COVID complications, but unlike another Cannes filmmaker who resurrected from near-death only to make bad art, the Russian auteur’s riveting comeback “Minotaur” is not only a return to form — it’s also exactly the kind of hopeless, coldly gazing, and politically indicting film only the director of “Leviathan” and “Loveless” could ever make.

Based on Claude Chabrol’s 1969 erotic thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” which itself inspired Adrian Lyne’s deliciously lurid adaptation “Unfaithful” with Diane Lane in 2022, “Minotaur” follows a feckless, selfish man down a dark rabbit hole of his own digging amid the news that his wife is having an affair. We’ve seen this story before, and we know where it’s going. But Zvyagintsev, with a camera as still and gimlet-eyed as the Sphinx except when it’s gliding through the saddest rooms in the world like a seeking serpent, delivers an outcome and a movie more hopeless and on-brand than you could’ve dreamed of. His screenplay, co-written by Simon Lyashenko, is as tight as a drum, or as a rug you wrap up a dead body inside. Related Stories Cary Grant, Clint Eastwood, and Christian Bale: The Stars Who Almost Played James Bond Robert Pattinson as James Bond Proves That IP Is No Longer the New Movie Stars

Even without knowing the plot of Chabrol’s or Lyne’s film, you know everybody is doomed to their own resigned lot in life when you’re in a Zvyagintsev picture, the same director who tore an already estranged couple apart with the disappearance of their son in “Loveless,” only for the boy never to be found because, well, that’s life under Mother Russia.

But in the Russia of “Minotaur,” which was actually shot in Latvia because the days of shooting politically trenchant material in Russia are done, Gleb Morozov (Dmitriy Mazurov) is the CEO of a shipping company. He lives in a Russian suburb, ensconced from life’s daily horrors, in a modernist home made of glass, steel, fine wood, and concrete. It’s autumn 2022, and Russia is mobilizing into Ukraine, with the town’s mayor mandating that Gleb assemble a list of his employees to be drafted into service. Videos of bombings, meanwhile, are entering people’s social media feeds.

Life at home for his wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) is an empty chain of days; she’s an unemployed housewife whose existence revolves around getting their son Seriosha (Boris Kudrin) to school on time. A woman for whom getting the right presents and ordering the right food for his birthday party is a full-time job to fill the vacant space of a day. But as “Minotaur” quite quickly reveals, she’s having an affair with a 33-year-old photographer, Anton (Yuriy Zavalnyouk), whom she visits almost daily under the guise of yet another appointment. It’s something to live for, a thrilling escape from a miserable life of staring into the void, waiting for her husband and son to come home.

Lebedeva, who is astonishing here, feels less like a doomed Chabrol heroine than someone cut out of Antonioni. A forcefield of ennui with an elegant trenchcoat around her, and with the furtive glee that comes with having a secret, she makes her way a few times a week down the road to her assignations with a younger, virile artist in the sort of apartment where a woman as beautiful and rich as this would ordinarily never deign to be.

It’s no secret to the audience that Gleb, who has a history of infidelity and jealousy, is going to find out what she’s up to, nor is it a shock how he reacts. It’s mildly frustrating that Zvyagintsev, for his first film in nine years and after a brush with death, chose material that is very much familiar to his already savvy cinephile audience.

But the thrill of “Minotaur” is in how the filmmaker repositions the inevitable violence wrought from being cuckolded, the stuff we recognize from classic noir movies, into the political context of life in Russia amid its invasion into Ukraine. Imagine a Hitchcock thriller situated in the saddest, crummiest, most totalitarian corners of our times — and with an unfliching camera that offers no reassurance — and you’ll have some idea of just how bleak this unfeeling movie can get.

Mikhail Krichman, cinematographer on all Zvyagintsev’s films, returns on “Minotaur” with a glacial, widescreen gaze that encourages the viewer to examine everything around them. There’s a hypnotizing 360-shot that starts with Galina and Anton day-drinking and then getting into bed, with composers Evgueni and Sacha Galperine’s worrying score pressing upon them, only to come back to the pair in an unchanged, postcoital position. But they can’t stop what’s coming to them, which is nothing good.

Zvyagintsev loves a red herring almost as much as a cosmically depressing visual joke, like the tiny picture of Putin hanging over a boardroom. Or the detectives who eventually show up at Gleb and Galina’s house, only to later look at some serious hard evidence that could solve their wild goose case and instead think, eh, let’s just go to lunch. Or this film’s last shot, which does not leave the viewer in an easy state of mind despite the comforting falsities that its characters embrace as they float above it all.

Zvyagintsev’s latest film, like all of his others from the fraught father-son journey of “The Return” to the slinking, snaky noir of “Elena,” is devoid of easy resolution, least of all hope. It may feel too familiar to those who have followed this filmmaker’s work closely, but “Minotaur” is capable of crushing you with its final suite of images that refuse to let you forget that the world we are living in is hell.

The actors are exquisite, transcending whatever allegorical mouthpieces you might read into them as, like when Lebedeva’s Galina, absolutely wasted after not hearing back from Anton for at least 24 hours and then drinking an entire bottle of wine at a bar, berates her son and husband for ordering the same old shit for dinner every night when she’s not cooking. Margherita pizza, margherita pizza. “Where is me?” she yells at the husband she feels nothing for. The husband who has been instructing their son how to bash in the faces of bullies who come at him at school.

“Minotaur” isn’t the best movie of Zvyagintsev’s career, but the icily exacting power of his filmmaking is undeniable — and it sucks you in like a vortex. Rarely are you so glued to a tale you’ve heard so many times before. Andrey Zvyagintsev, welcome back. We missed, and we need you.

“Minotaur” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release the film later this year.
