#3426. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3424. ‘Rivals’ Season 2 Boss Reveals the Meaning Behind That Rupert and Taggie Scene in Episode 9 [Exclusive]

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for Episodes 7-9 of Rivals Season 2.Fans of Rupert (Alex Hassell) and Taggie (Bella Maclean) were dealt another blow at the end of Rivals Season 2, Episode 9 last Wednesday, when Rupert pulled away just as the pair seemed poised to kiss. With Episode 10 and the much-anticipated Hunt Ball on the horizon, a little more yearning seems like just what the doctor ordered for these two. Speaking with Collider, Rivals executive producer Alex Lamb explained why these pivotal Rupert and Taggie scenes needed to bookend the episode and what they mean for the pair’s burgeoning relationship.

Episode 8 ended with a shocking reveal as Maud (Victoria Smurfit) and Tony’s (David Tennant) affair finally came to light. The episode, already full of fireworks and explosions thanks to Bonfire Night, culminated in a violent and very public fight between Maud and Declan (Aidan Turner) as Declan revealed to his Venturer pals that Maud has been the one leaking secrets to Tony the entire time.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

Of course, we learn later from Tony that the mole is, in fact, male and therefore can't be Maud. But before that big twist, Venturer lies in shambles at the beginning of Episode 9. Maud is staying above Bar Sinister, while Declan wakes up in a pile of trash after a night of binge drinking. When Bas (Luca Pasqualino) brings him back to the O’Haras home, it feels like all hope is lost. Caitlin (Catriona Chandler) is going back to school, devastated by the idea that her parents might actually split up. Not only that, but the franchise seems to be Corinium's to win as Tony uses Monica's (Claire Rushbrook) death as an emotional crutch to explain his publicized dalliance with Maud.

Episode 9 then sees Rupert and Declan come together to try and fix their problems and get Venturer back on track. They fly to New York to win Cameron (Nafessa Williams) back after her breakup with Rupert, and Declan brings the IBA board out to Penscombe to show off their greatest strengths as they present the board with their brand-new TV ideas complete with a musical performance, a delicious lunch, and a robot-made martini to boot!

The impetus for all of this comes when Taggie decides to bring the application straight to Rupert's door, pushing him to fix the mess that her parents have made. Set to an instrumental version of Bonnie Tyler’s “Holding Out for a Hero," she shows up at Penscombe not to cry about the state of her home life or in search of a knight in shining armor, but to push Rupert to do what he does best: win.

While the scene at the end of the episode might leave "Rutag" shippers a bit disappointed that even after all of that, the two haven't reconciled, Lamb still calls the scenes "the spine of the episode." In both this first scene between Rupert and Taggie at Penscombe and the last one, we not only get a development of their current rocky relationship, but are once again reminded about Taggie's impact on Rupert. Lamb explains, "We felt we needed to up Rupert and Taggie's story and have that be the bookend around that push of the Venturer plot and how we are going to pull Declan out of the doldrums."

There are worse things in store than laxatives and escaping naked out of a bathroom window.

Rupert and Taggie have been avoiding each other since Monica’s funeral, when he called her "childish" while still reeling from having witnessed Monica’s death firsthand. But Lamb explains that the Episode 9 scenes are vital for their relationship. "It felt very important to us that we had a really strong, inciting incident for Rupert and Taggie to go, 'Right, we have been apart from each other. There's been unpleasantness between us,' but now the chips are down, Taggie knows the only person that can help her dad is [Rupert]."

It's because of Taggie's plea that Rupert goes on his journey across town with her to find Declan, leading them to an ominous encounter with Tony and Beattie (Annabel Scholey), where he once again tries to tear the team apart — though this time without much success. After that, both men are pushed to get their vengeance against Tony, delivering a standout performance for the IBA and proving that Venturer is still a horse worth betting on in this race.

#3423. ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Returning to Theaters with a New Rosario Dawson Cameo — and Box Office Records and Oscar Noms in Mind

Usually this is the time of year when early-year and summer awards contenders come back to theaters (see: “The Odyssey”). But even though it only left theaters not long ago, Sony is re-releasing “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which is now the biggest domestic release of all time.

The studio is bringing the film back to theaters on December 4, with tickets going on sale November 19. And the new version will be an extended cut of the film (cheekily titled “Spider-Man: [Brand New] Brand New Day”) that will feature one deleted scene in which Rosario Dawson stars as a character called The Night Nurse. Director Daniel Destin Cretton had previously told press that she shot a scene for the film that was cut. Related Stories ‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Riveting Comeback Remakes Claude Chabrol and ‘Unfaithful’ for a Hopeless Wartime Russia Cary Grant, Clint Eastwood, and Christian Bale: The Stars Who Almost Played James Bond

The real reason “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is coming back to theaters is because it gives the film yet another chance to add on to its record box office haul. Maybe it surpasses $1 billion domestic? It’s only $41 million shy, and the re-release of “Avengers Endgame: Encore” managed to gross $40 million domestic, so there’s a real chance of that. It also turns out that Sony really does view the film as an awards contender and thinks it deserves to be back top of mind. SPE chief Tom Rothman recently told Deadline that the studio was launching an FYC campaign for the film and believed “Brand New Day” worthy of a Best Picture nomination.

“If there aren’t people thinking about it, we’re gonna do what we can just to make people think about it,” Rothman said. “I think it’s also incumbent upon studios who make these kinds of quality commercial films to get people to think about it, and here’s what I ask people when I walk around: ‘Are you telling me that there are 10 films this year that are better than this film?’”

The only other new studio wide release on December 4 is “Violent Night 2,” so it’s a relatively light weekend in what figures to be an incredibly crowded Christmas box office, one that even includes Sony’s own “Jumanji: Open World” and of course “Avengers: Doomsday” the weekend prior.

#3422. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3420. 54 Years Ago, Peanuts Went From Meh To Masterpiece With Just One Comic

Volumes have been written about what makes Peanuts great. And rightly so. But what about the moment when Peanuts became great? That's a different story. What was the comic where things really clicked for Charles M. Schulz? Where Peanuts leveled up and officially became what it was destined to be? It all goes back to a small but significant milestone for the strip's unexpected breakout hit character: Snoopy.

The Peanuts Gang never grew up. They might have celebrated birthdays now and then, but they never got older. They never matured. They did, however, evolve, especially early in the strip's 50-year run. And no character evolved faster, or more significantly, than Snoopy. The black-and-white beagle started out as a canine companion, a scrappy sidekick for Charlie Brown. By 2000, when Peanuts ended, Snoopy was the star of the show, and arguably had the most developed personality out of the whole Gang.

Over time, Snoopy's internal monologue became a Peanuts staple. It became familiar to readers to watch him react in his head, via thought balloon, to something Charlie Brown, or Lucy, or Linus just said. Or to carry on entire, one-sided conversations with himself. Or to lapse into fantasy entirely, imagining himself as a World War I pilot or a famous writer. Snoopy's interior life became more fleshed out than many of Peanuts' more ancillary characters.

To get to that point, there had to be a first time Snoopy had a thought. Or otherwise, the first time the audience was privy to what Snoopy was thinking. It might have just been a fun wrinkle for Charles Schulz to throw into the mix at the time, but it wound up having a profound effect on Peanuts, helping seal its place in pop culture in perpetuity.

It is May 1952. Peanuts has been running for about a year and a half. It is still trying to get its syndication numbers up to 50 newspapers across the United States. The strip has steady momentum. Back in January, it started running extra-sized Sunday strips, a signal that publisher United Features Syndicate and the editors at the papers that bought Peanuts believed in it.

It is a milestone year creatively too. Lucy van Pelt debuts in March. Linus, her brother, first appears later that fall. The catchphrase "good grief" pops up for the first time. The infamous "football gag" starts before the end of the year. And Snoopy, most of all, becomes a main cast member. That starts in May, when his interiority is depicted for the first time.

Originally, Snoopy looked quite different from the droopy-eared, peanut-headed icon he's known as today, starring in a beautifully minimalistic strip.

Before considering the moment everything changed for Snoopy, it is worth putting his look under the microscope. In '52, the beagle is still barely more than a doodle of a dog. He hasn't taken on his more recognizable form yet. That's still a few years off. So, to get all philosophical for a moment, like Peanuts was occasionally prone to, existence preceded essence for Snoopy, but once he gained the essential component of an interior monologue, he was finally able to evolve into the beloved pop culture icon that has existed ever since.

May 27, 1952. It is a Tuesday. Readers in 40-45 newspapers, from Allentown, Pennsylvania to Seattle, Washington open up the funny pages to find this strip. In the first frame, Snoopy sits serenely on the lawn, minding his own business. In the second panel, along comes Charlie Brown, humming some tune to himself. In panel three, Charlie Brown playfully tugs on Snoopy's ear and says, "kind of warm out today for ear muffs, isn't it?"

It is a dumb joke. A childish joke. Which makes sense. It is made by a child. But it is playful, and innocent enough. It is a joke, but it isn't this Peanuts strip's punchline. Instead, it is the set-up for the punchline, which comes in the final frame. For readers at the time, in '52, it would have been a delightful surprise. Snoopy can speak like a human! Or at least, think like one.

"Why do I have to suffer such indignities?" Snoopy thinks, walking away in a huff. The dog's thought bubble is a squiggly line, perhaps to convey that Snoopy is rattled by the interaction, or maybe just to visually differentiate it from the human Peanuts characters' dialogue. Either way, that stylistic touch wouldn't last, but what would is the portrayal of Snoopy as not just thinking complex human thoughts, but having complex human emotions.

Sure, Snoopy would become a bit more Zen as time went on, but he also demonstrated a temper at times. In this gamechanging Peanuts comic, he's indignant at having his idyllic moment interrupted. The foundations of Snoopy's long-term character had already been laid by the time Charles M. Schulz decided to give him an internal voice; that decision allowed Schulz to build Snoopy up from there in ways that never would have been possible otherwise.

Within a few years of Snoopy's first thought, Peanuts exploded in popularity. The strip went from appearing in dozens of newspapers to hundreds. It got media attention, as a result of its exponential growth and developing fandom. Snoopy's voice, and Snoopy's personality, were arguably the missing pieces of the puzzle that pushed Peanuts from good to great, from "meh" to masterpiece.

Another big moment for Snoopy in '52 was the first time he danced, something that would become a key part of his character when the Peanuts Gang made the jump to TV in the 1960s. It was another step toward humanizing him as a character. In turn, it was another level of depth added to Peanuts, opening up a whole new world of jokes for the series to make. So, this was a pivotal moment for more than just furthering the strip's appeal to readers. It was also critical to the longevity of Peanuts.

The Peanuts have many classic comics that are amazing, but here are seven comic strips related to Snoopy that are genuine 10/10 masterpieces.

It might not have been immediately evident as a "level up" moment for Peanuts, but in retrospect, it is the moment that Charles M. Schulz figured up the missing ingredient to his series and compensated. It was when Schulz solidified his place, and his characters' place, in the pop culture canon forever.

#3419. ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

A very successful “values-based entertainment” company that was begat — in the parlance of its biblical heritage — from a film-filtering service that illegally edited “objectionable content” out of major Hollywood movies, Angel Studios has since become the world’s foremost purveyor of megachurch-approved multiplex content. The bigger they got (on the strength of projects like “The Chosen” and the QAnon cause célèbre “Sound of Freedom,” the latter of which pioneered a questionable ticketing model that continues today), the more that Angel removed from the films they released. Not just sex and swear words, but also anything that even vaguely resembled a soul. Related Stories ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Returning to Theaters with a New Rosario Dawson Cameo — and Box Office Records and Oscar Noms in Mind ‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Riveting Comeback Remakes Claude Chabrol and ‘Unfaithful’ for a Hopeless Wartime Russia

With “Hershey,” a decidedly vanilla biopic about the most famous chocolatier who’s ever lived, the studio has taken its socio-religious project to its logical conclusion: They’ve made a movie that’s been stripped of any flavor whatsoever. It’s the cinematic equivalent of carob powder. It’s what Ned Flanders will force his kids to watch next Halloween.

Somehow unimaginatively bland and Splenda-sweet all at once, this godforsaken affront to good storytelling may not have benefited from any of the material that its distributor has deemed amoral, but “Hershey” is so mind-numbingly absent the most basic friction of the human experience that I wanted to fall to my knees and thank the lord that a few errant Kisses made it past The Angel Promise on a technicality. It’s too bad Milton S. Hershey never used his platform to baselessly sow doubt in a foreign election, because at least one of Angel Studios’ co-founders would clearly have been cool with including that (ecocidal fascism is fine, just don’t say “fuck” while you’re razing the Amazon, as that would offend Jesus).

As you may have gathered by now, I am probably not the target audience for this unrepentant godslop.

Not because I’m agnostic (“Hershey” is as secular as Angel Studios’ output gets, its overt religiosity limited to a brief scene in which the movie’s namesake pleads for help from an unspecified higher power), but rather because I stubbornly, blasphemously insist that a womb-to-tomb biopic should bear at least some faint resemblance to the stuff of real life. I couldn’t possibly care less about the facts (though I struggle to believe that Hershey and his wife literally danced with joy after learning that a twist of fate had spared them from being aboard the Titanic), but there isn’t a single moment in this film that feels like it was written by a real person, let alone lived by one.

Let’s back up a beat. To be clear, Angel Studios didn’t technically make this movie — that distinction belongs to the spiritually aligned production company Dandelion Media, who partnered with Hershey Entities for a fully authorized feature-length commercial meant to “bring [the chocolate brand’s] story into culture in a more immersive way.” The success of that marketing spend remains to be seen, but it can’t hurt to highlight Mr. Hershey’s ostensible purity at a time when the company that bears his name has been under fire for diluting its products with compound coatings in order to save money. And so we have a punishingly straightforward film that paints the Pennsylvania icon as a square-jawed, sweet-toothed wife guy who loved candy, orphans, and sitting way too close to the edge of the massive water tower that overlooks the town he remade in his own image.

Directed by Mark Waters, but absent any trace of the poppy confidence he once brought to the likes of “Mean Girls” and “Freaky Friday,” “Hershey” opens with its first and only stylistic flourish as a match cut transforms an immaculate chocolate Kiss into a small lump of coal — Milton Hershey’s life would turn out to be sweet, but it sure didn’t start that way. The film that follows sadly feels less like “Lawrence of Arabia” than it does an AI-generated adaptation of Hershey’s Wikipedia page, its algorithmic sense of human interaction rendered all the more uncanny by its ecclesiastical approach to conflict (and also by its blown out cinematography, which suggests a very literal interpretation of Angel Studios’ promise to produce “movies and shows that amplify light.”)

Adhering to the prosaic structure and candied morality that the Erwin brothers have made endemic to the world of faith-based biopics and their immediate kin, the film sees Hershey’s life as a blessed march towards his eternal reward — one that’s only slowed down by the litany of speed bumps that pop up along his path to heaven.

Young Milton’s very serious Mennonite mom is a major bummer, but she lets him out of the house to work for a local printer. The JRPG-like town where he grows up in the 1860s seems inhospitable to dreams, but its muddy roads make it appear as though the streets are paved with chocolate. His dad (Alan Ruck, a long way from “Succession”) abandons him pretty fast, but not before bending down to the kid like Zooey Deschanel in “Almost Famous” and telling him: “You’re a Hershey, and that means when you follow your dream, you don’t let anyone get in your way.” Apparently his dad’s dream was to not live with his family anymore, but so be it. A good example is a good example.

Every stumbling block is immediately followed by a burst of divine providence, as Sharon Paul and Timothy Michael Hayes’ script adheres to the grindset mindset of the prosperity gospel while Rolfe Kent’s saccharine score blends everything together into a tasteless slurry of unrefined sugar. The film insists that a little sweetness goes a long way, as an orgasmic taste of rock candy is all that Milton needs to make it through the day, but it doesn’t heed its own advice. Milton’s passion leads him to a job working for a saintly confectioner named Joseph Royer (a beneficent Richard Kind, as close to a live-action Bing Bong as he’s ever been), who just smiles it off when the kid forgets to turn off the peanut roaster and nearly burns down the whole shop.

Later, after sprouting into Finn Wittrock and starting his own caramel company, Milton is miraculously spared from ruin several times over by virtue of his non-denominational faith in himself and the universe. One low moment is redeemed by a massive order from overseas. Another resolves with a traveling salesman busting into the Lancaster Caramel Company with an offer to invest in chocolate — the future of snacking! “This chocolate,” Milton sniffs, “it could be good if it wasn’t so bad.” I know the feeling. The next time disaster strikes, he inadvertently stumbles upon the Hershey Kiss in the very next scene. The plotting is schematic enough to make “Bohemian Rhapsody” seem like “Last Days” by comparison.

Somewhere in there Milton enjoys a meet-cute with a woman named Kitty Sweeney (Alexandria Daddario), a grinning beauty who credits caramels with curing her shyness. Her job as Milton’s wife is to be his biggest cheerleader, and then — as the years melt away — to collapse in undiagnosed pain whenever he leaves the room. At one point it is implied that she and Milton have sexual intercourse, but only so the movie can leverage the couple’s inability to conceive a child into a robust philanthropic regime that allowed them to house and educate any number of white male orphans.

Of course, expecting this movie to acknowledge the Milton Hershey School’s history of racial and social discrimination would be as delusional as thinking its third act might address the labor disputes that unsettled Hershey’s chocolate factory in the late 1930s. Such things are simply not sweet enough to befit a story about how some vague belief and a little stick-it-to-em are all a man needs to prosper in this great land — even if a warts-and-all version of that same story would still be a model of American success.

Considerably less textured than the chocolate bars that have become synonymous with its title character, Waters’ film is so determined to launder one man’s dreams into reality that it comes to assume its own kind of dream logic in return — one divorced from the basic relationship between cause-and-effect or an event and its meaning.

In what might be the single most deranged movie scene of the year, Milton and his ailing wife Kitty literally dance for joy on the bow of a ship after learning that a twist of fate has spared them from being aboard the Titanic, even though upwards of 1,400 other people went to a watery grave that night. I’m not sure that qualifies as bringing the brand’s “story into the culture in a more immersive way,” but it’s definitely what I’m going to be thinking about the next time I bite into a milky and delicious Hershey Bar. After watching this perversely chalky film about the company’s founder, it’s a wonder that I can still remember what their signature product even tastes like.

Angel Studios will release “Hershey” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

#3417. What to Expect From Best Buy's 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales

For all intents and purposes, Black Friday sales are already here. There are plenty of deals out already, even though we're weeks away from the actual event. One of the reasons for that is the competition retailers have with each other to be the first to get your money. One of the retailers that is making the biggest early splash is Best Buy, confirming their entire plan for the rest of the year. Here's what you need to know.

Best Buy has announced the following events:

DoorBoosters: A Halloween sale from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1.

Early Black Friday Deals and Doorbusters: The official start of early Black Friday deals on Nov. 6. New deals will drop every Friday.

Black Friday Doorbusters and Deals: Best Buy says this will be its main sale, starting on Thursday, Nov. 19 and running until Nov. 28 with deals on "computing, gaming, home theater, wearables, and more."

Cyber Sunday and Monday: Best Buy is extending Cyber Monday to five days and says you can find deals going up to 50% off select tech.

Last-minute savings: The Christmas sale will run from Dec. 18 until Dec. 24.

You don't need to be any kind of member to shop Best Buy's Black Friday in July sale; however, it is free to sign up for a My Best Buy membership, which will get you free shipping. If you join one of their paid subscriptions (My Best Buy Plus for $49.99 per year or My Best Buy Total for $179.99 per year), you'll get faster free shipping, exclusive prices and deals, an extended 60-day return window on most products, and access to select sales, like the Member Deals Days sale that is going on right now. Paid members will also earn extra rewards from both the current sale and the upcoming Black Friday in July sale.

You can find deals on TVs, laptops, headphones, video games, electric bikes, and more. There will be new deals every week in stores, on its website, and in the Best Buy mobile app. They'll offer price matching, meaning if the price drops further during the sale (Dec. 24), they will match it and offer a refund.

Here are the best deals I've found so far. I'll be updating these deals throughout the sale, so make sure to come back and see what's new. Remember that new deals drop every day.

Best Buy price matches its own products, so if a product drops in price later, you'd get those savings too, but it does not cover any deals coming from a competitor's Black Friday sale. There are some other important exceptions you can read in more detail here.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

The other major retailers doing Black Friday sales are Amazon, Target, and Walmart. Currently, Amazon has many early deals, seeing their lowest prices yet. Target has some week-long deals and a Deal of the Day. Walmart will have three Black Friday and Cyber Monday shopping events. Nowadays, large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3416. 7 Forgotten Netflix Miniseries That Are Perfect From Start to Finish

Content Warning: This list contains a brief mention of sexual assault.Netflix is highly known for its original productions, which include many compelling miniseries. Its hits include The Queen's Gambit, Baby Reindeer, and Adolescence, all of which are award-winning masterpieces. Some of the streaming platform's miniseries were also responsible for skyrocketing actors to stardom through debut or breakout roles, including Owen Cooper for his portrayal of Jamie Miller in Adolescence and Victoria Pedretti for playing Danielle "Dani" Clayton in The Haunting of Bly Manor.

Netflix has shown no sign of slowing down its miniseries productions, and is already planning to drop more next year. However, like many of the streaming platform's critically acclaimed miniseries, the shows could go from record-breaking hits, to fan-favorite series in the "Bingeworthy TV Shows" section in less than six months. With that in mind, here are forgotten Netflix miniseries that are perfect from start to finish.

Maniac is the perfect miniseries for when someone is looking to watch a combination of a science fiction and psychological drama series. The show centers around Annie Landsberg (Emma Stone) and Owen Milgrim (Jonah Hill), and the hallucinations they begin to have while experiencing the effects of the intense pharmaceutical trial that is being overseen by Dr. James K. Mantleray (Josh Theroux), and Dr. Azumi Fujita (Sonoya Mizuno) of Neberdine Pharmaceutical Biotech (NPB). Annie and Owen were attracted to the trial after learning the point of it was to cure all psychological disorders, but neither of them had no idea what they'd be doing until the trial began.

Stone and Hill's acting matured quite a bit in the years since they starred in Superbad together, and it was easy to see during their portrayals of a woman with borderline personality disorder, and a man with schizophrenia. The dedication they had while portraying their characters was felt throughout every episode, and the smiles their characters had in the final scene was the perfect finishing touch for the miniseries, and their portrayals. Although the miniseries was not an award winner, it did debut in the 10 most-watched Netflix shows list, and stayed there for almost a week.

Alias Grace is an adaption of the 1996 novel written by Margaret Atwood, who first gained prominence in the entertainment industry for writing The Handmaid's Tale. The miniseries centers around Grace Marks (Sarah Gadon), a housemaid convicted of murder and discusses her story with a psychiatrist named Dr. Simon Jordan (Edward Holcroft). The more she explained her friend and family background to her psychiatrist, the harder it got for viewers to believe she deserved to be in prison for the rest of her life.

The show was highly praised by critics, who gave the miniseries a 99% on Rotten Tomatoes for its plot lines and characters. Gadon did a tremendous job in bringing her character's complexity to the screen, which allowed audiences to get to know Grace, a grieving victim of abuse, not Grace, the woman accused of murdering Thomas Kinnear (Paul Gross), and Nancy Montgomery (Anna Paquin), with co-conspirator, James McDermott (Kerr Logan). Although her character was pardoned, audiences will always wonder what motivated Grace to kill Thomas and Nancy, if she was indeed the murderer.

Based on the 2008-2011 Washington and Colorado serial rape cases, Unbelievable is both a painful and must-watch miniseries, especially for women. The show starts with Marie Adler (Kaitlyn Dever), a victim of a brutal rape who is ultimately arrested for what police claim was "false reporting." In the meantime, detectives Grace Rasmussen (Toni Collette) and Karen Duvall (Merritt Wever) work to catch a serial rapist, and through their work, they find the truth, and fight to bring justice to all his victims, including Marie.

Collette and Wever's performances were an inspiration, and the fierceness they brought to their characters proved they were the right actresses for the roles of detectives seeking the truth. Dever's was just as phenomenal, and she made her character grow stronger every episode, showing viewers they too could find the strength to keep going forward, and not look back. It was stunning to see that the miniseries did not take home Emmys or Golden Globes, but Collette took home a Critics Choice Award, and the show won a Peabody Award.

Based on a true story featured in the 2012 book Unorthodox: The Scandalous Rejection of My Hasidic Roots, Unorthodox is a touching miniseries about ultra-Orthodox community member Esther "Esty" Shapiro (Shira Haas) working to rebuild her life in Berlin after leaving her husband, Yaakov "Yanky" Shapiro (Amit Rahav), with whom she's had an unhappy marriage. Esty's husband, along with his cousin, Moses "Moishe" Lefkovitch (Jeff Wilbusch), travel to Berlin to find Esty, and bring her home to their community in New York. She eventually decides to try and earn a scholarship to a music conservatory, and stops at nothing to do so.

Haas' portrayal of Esty was her international breakthrough, and it was the determination she brought out in her character that made fans realize they could have the life they deserve. Her vocals were also incredible, and to hear her character say she was not allowed to sing out loud in her community made her performance even more powerful and tear-jerking. Haas became the first Israeli actress to be nominated for a Primetime Emmy for her role, and the show has since been considered to be one of the greatest Netflix miniseries of all time.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Ripley centers around Tom Ripley (Andrew Scott), a petty con-artist turned murderer who takes advantage of someone's mistake to attempt to bring home the spoiled, Dickie Greenleaf (Johnny Flynn) from Italy. He meets Dickie and his girlfriend, Marge Sherwood, (Dakota Fanning), and is introduced to the lavish lifestyle the pair have for themselves in Atrani. Things take a dark turn early on, and the con man's cockiness builds as he continues to get away with the lies he's told.

The decision to film this 1960s-based miniseries in black and white makes this memorable, as show runner, Steven Zaillian, and cinematographer, Robert Elswitt, wanted to pay tribute to the original novel. Even if it wasn't filmed in black and white, Ripley would still be memorable for its stars' performances, especially by Scott and Fanning. The personalities each actor brought out in their characters were unbeatable, and the miniseries has since become one of the only psychological thriller miniseries that are perfect from beginning to end.

Bill Skarsgård did not mess around while portraying a condescending criminal in the 2022 miniseries Clark. The series is based on the life of Clark Olofsson, a Swedish gangster with the desire to "be his best at being the worst." The series mainly chronicles the crimes he committed over the years, including the events of the Norrmalmstorg robbery, which created the well-known term "Stockholm Syndrome."

It was unsurprising to see Skarsgård in this role due to his phenomenal performances in horror productions, but his tremendous portrayal of the twisted criminal made viewers have a hard time not believing the actor himself was a conceited sociopath. Critics and audiences loved Clark, which is why it's shocking that the show did not debut in the top 10 most-watched Netflix shows list at the time of its release. Although its popularity diminished years ago, it still led to Skarsgård winning a Kristallen Award for his performance.

Not only is Pluto a spin-off of the hit manga Astro-Boy, it's also one of the highest-rated anime shows on Netflix. The show centers around a string of murdered robots and humans in a futuristic world, and how the victims' connections to one another turn the investigation's intensity up to a whole new level. As the miniseries progresses, the investigation turns into a fight to end the cycle of hatred, and save more lives in the process.

It's difficult to find an anime show on Netflix that can only work if themes like grief and PTSD are addressed. These themes were introduced beautifully by the characters, and the actors' stayed true to every character until the end. Although Pluto is not an award-winning miniseries, it's still an emotional one that shows fans the importance of choosing love over hate, especially toward their peers.

#3414. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3405. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3400. iPhone Duo one week later: The future, or not for me?

My iPhone Duo arrived last Thursday, so I’ve had a week to use it as my daily carry. My early experience has been mixed, so I keep asking myself an important question: is this the iPhone’s future and I just need to adapt, or is the Duo simply not for everyone?

After a week using the iPhone Duo, in some ways I have a lot of clarity about the product, and in other ways my thinking is very clouded.

To put it simply: I’m not having a great time with the Duo, which makes me wonder if the problem is me, not it.

I’ve seen countless social media posts from Duo owners proclaiming how much they love the product. And I absolutely believe them. The iPhone Duo is a remarkable innovation for the iPhone. It’s cool, weird, and wonderful in all sorts of ways. But for me and my needs (preferences?), it’s been more frustrating than enjoyable.

And that frustration mainly boils down to one thing: I almost never want to open it.

I’d estimate at least 90% of my iPhone Duo usage involves the front display. And when I unfold it the remaining 10% of the time, it’s often because I force myself to do it in the hopes of discovering what I’m missing out on. Like, I know I should be unfolding it more, so I do. But it doesn’t add any real value for me.

Because I rarely want to open the iPhone Duo, I’m left using the outer display all the time. In that mode, the Duo is too heavy for extended use, too wide to comfortably reach, and the UI in most apps is an adjustment.

Are these dealbreakers? No. I could live with the Duo’s outer display if I had to, but it’s definitely an inferior experience to my iPhone 18 Pro.

If I was opening the iPhone Duo more, and actually taking advantage of the key value proposition of foldables—that you can unfold them—I doubt the outer screen would bother me much.

But what I’ve found, at least so far, is that one-handed iPhone use is very important to me, which rules out using the inner display. I use my iPhone mostly for quick interactions, and often with a child in one hand (I have three very young kids). In situations when I do have two hands free to open the Duo, I’m probably sitting in front of my iPad Pro with a Magic Keyboard attached and would rather use the iPad instead.

So again: is the problem with the Duo, or with me?

I think foldables and slab phones will obviously coexist as there will be fans of each.

I’m absolutely already converted however and am loving my duo.

Considering the Air was my favourite phone up until this it’s surprised me. I love proper one handed use again on the outside screen and unfolded it’s much nicer than my old mini 7.

I get it’s not for everyone but those that click with it like myself have a superb device!

I think it’s the latter, but I’m not sure “problem” is the right word. I just don’t find myself using it the way it’s meant to be used. And that’s fine.

I want to love the iPhone Duo, because I see how much fun other people are having with it. And maybe given more time, something will click and I’ll start to use it “as intended.”

If iPhone Duo is the future of the iPhone, I’ll adapt and move on with my life. But one week in, I think it’s probably just not for me. And if it’s not for me, maybe there are a lot of people who will continue preferring non-foldable iPhones for many years to come.

What’s your iPhone Duo experience been like? Are you loving it or struggling? Let us know in the comments.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3398. The Grammy Nominations Blanked Harry Styles. What Happened?

The Grammy nominations today are full of surprises — but the big shocker is the name that isn’t there. Harry Styles got zero nods for his acclaimed album Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally. The last time he dropped an album, Harry’s House, it won Album of the Year, while his single “As It Was” got nominated for Song and Record of the Year. In January, he released KissCo, a deeply personal and experimental statement — but also a wildly successful hit, debuting at Number One and spawning the chart-topping “Aperture.” Yet it got no Grammy nominations at all. How did this happen?

You can practically hear fans around the world asking the Grammys: What kind of pills are you on? (Not the good ones, that’s for sure.)

It can’t be overstated how weird this is. Michael J. Fox got a Grammy nomination. Shaggy got one. So did Fred Armisen, Michelle Obama, Frank Zappa, Tim Curry. There’s Queen Latifah and the Pixies’ Black Francis — in the country category. But not Harry Styles. Hell, even Kanye West got nominated for Best Rap Album — who thinks West had a more successful year making music than Styles? The Recording Academy, that’s who.

The album was submitted in the major pop categories, including Album of the Year and Pop Vocal Album. “Aperture” was submitted for Record, Song, Pop Solo Performance, Music Video — all categories where he’s been nominated before. “Coming Up Roses” was submitted for Best Arrangement; the Netflix special One Night in Manchester for Best Music Film. (KissCo was also submitted for Album Cover, but this year’s nominees are tough to explain — Charli XCX and Slayyyter got shut out too.) Where Styles didn’t submit was the Dance Pop categories, or even Rock, which might have been easier going.

But this is just a drastic break with Grammy history. In the past 50 years, when any artist wins Album of the Year, they get nominated for their next album, in some category or another. It’s almost unheard of for them to get shut out next time. It’s happened only three times: Mumford & Sons won AOTY in 2013 (for Babel), Steely Dan in 2001 (for Two Against Nature), Toto in 1983 (for Toto IV). They all soon released follow-ups that got zero Grammy noms. But these follow-ups weren’t really comparable to KissCo — none of them hit Number One or included a Number One hit. So there’s no real precedent for this. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Every other Album of the Year winner got thrown a bone for their next studio album, with a nomination or two. That means Christopher Cross, Phil Collins, Natalie Cole, Tony Bennett, Norah Jones, George Michael, Celine Dion, Bob Dylan, Santana, OutKast, Herbie Hancock, Arcade Fire, Kacey Musgraves, Jon Batiste. But not Styles. (Obviously, there are a few Best Album winners where there wasn’t a follow-up, when the artist dies or quits or is Lauryn Hill.)

The Grammys tend to be legacy-minded, by definition — once the Academy decides you’re a Grammy type of artist, you remain a Grammy type of artist. There’s a certain “incumbent advantage.” Grammy voters are old, old, old, and they’d always rather vote for someone they’ve already voted for. His one-time opening act Kacey Musgraves won AOTY for Golden Hour, then put out a follow-up that nobody liked much, Star-Crossed — but still snagged a couple of country nominations for the song “Camera Roll.” That’s how it usually works. Not this time.

It’s even stranger since Harry has been a key part of the Grammy ceremony in recent years — at this year’s show, when Bad Bunny won Album of the Year, Harry was the one who handed it to him. It was the big dramatic climax of the night — who can forget Bad Bunny breaking down in tears at his table after hearing Harry read the name?

But it was hardly the first show-stealing turn for Styles, as in his “Watermelon Sugar” that kicked off the 2022 ceremony. He had to fight an uphill battle getting Grammy recognition, since he started out as the Academy’s absolute least favorite kind of artist — a singer in a boy band, a British one no less, who formed on TV for a reality show, tsk-tsk. But the Academy eventually caught on to what the audience already knew, recognizing him with his first Grammy for “Watermelon Sugar.” He became one of the first winners in history to give his acceptance speech wearing a feather boa — a very Harry touch. Related Content Dolly Parton Competes Against Herself in One of the 2027 Grammys’ Country Categories Don’t Be Surprised That BTS Aren’t Nominated for the 2027 Grammys Will Miranda Lambert Break the Producer of the Year Glass Ceiling? Beyoncé Makes History as First Artist to Earn 100 Grammy Award Nominations

Kiss All the Time has been acclaimed as one of the year’s boldest and best albums, moving way out of the Harry’s House comfort zone where he easily could have stayed. It’s not a universal pop crowd-pleaser like Harry’s House, without any undeniable radio blockbuster like “As It Was” or “Adore You” or “Watermelon Sugar.” It got plenty of bewildered first-week reviews, largely from people confused by the moody electroclash club sounds, misinterpreting the title to think this was the straight-up disco record it plainly wasn’t. So for many people, the music took time to appreciate. But it holds up to nine months of heavy listening, with bangers like “Dance No More” and “Ready, Steady, Go,” as well as intimate ballads like “Coming Up Roses” and “The Waiting Game.”

Styles chose not make the safe follow-up he could have cranked out in his sleep. He made sure nobody could mistake KissCo for Harry’s House Part 2: Better Homes and Gardens. That’s never been how he operates as an artist. He’s the guy who blew up in One Direction, yet made his solo move with a totally uncommercial and eccentric singer-songwriter statement, inspired by the Laurel Canyon 1970s. His debut solo single was “Sign of the Times,” a glam-rock piano epic about death, building for almost six minutes, conceding nothing to trends or the radio. A bold and brazen statement — but it proved him as an artist who was determined to go his own way, rather than chase anybody else’s idea of pop success.

That mindset has worked out for Harry, to say the least, after the astounding year he’s had in 2026. He’s been packing stadiums around the planet for his Together, Together Tour, with the innovation of playing multi-night residencies in a few cities. (He hasn’t made it to L.A. yet — is that why the Recording Academy didn’t notice?)

His 30-night run at Madison Square Garden — by this tour’s standards, the tiniest and most intimate of venues — was a career highlight, even when he wasn’t busting out the slutty shorts. But he’s kept the show evolving and changing as it travels, with so many ambitious peaks — in London, his orchestral performance with “Bridge Over Troubled Water,” or in New York, his indie-sleaze electro-punk detonation of “Kiwi.” He also had an unforgettable moment in one of the year’s biggest and best movies, Project Hail Mary, where the “Sign of the Times” karaoke scene is one of the year’s most poignant music moments.

If there’s anything we know about Styles, deeply private though he is, it’s that he’s just not interested in celebrity clichés. He’s not the kind of pop star who chases red carpets and award shows. Remember, last year on Oscar Night, he not only failed to show up, but he spent the day running the Tokyo Marathon without telling anyone he was doing it. (He did even better at the Berlin Marathon.) When he was in New York for his 10-week run at Madison Square Garden, he wouldn’t have been caught dead at a fancy club or party or gala. Instead, he simply walked to work every day, prowling the city streets with no handlers or entourage, just his trusty “Techno Is My Boyfriend” baseball cap. On the final night, the Garden gave him a banner to commemorate his record-breaking run of sold-out shows, presented by the Knicks’ Jalen Brunson. For this historic occasion, Harry was dressed as a pizza rat. Trending Stories Raye, Rosalía, and Ella Langley Lead 2027 Grammy Nominees Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’ Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Robert Pattinson Is the Next James Bond

The KissCo snub already looks like one of the great comic gaffes in Grammy history. But if winning Grammys were the kind of thing that interested Harry Styles, he’d be a very different kind of artist. But nearly 10 years into his solo career, he’s kept proving it over and over again — he’s a headstrong boy who does exactly what he wants, not what he thinks an audience will expect. He works with people he knows and trusts, not the buzziest pros, and he only releases music when he’s passionate about it, like his hero Thom Yorke. As he told Yorke this summer, in their Rolling Stone Musicians on Musicians cover story, “You have to just be, ‘What do I want to listen to at this time in my life? What is it that I feel like I want to do, say, make?’ And the fact that people are going to hear it — that realization happens later.”

That’s why he does everything from the heart — and that’s exactly why the audience has responded. It’s truly baffling that the Grammys missed out on a chance to be part of the KissCo story.

#3396. The Apple Watch's New 'Siri Recap' Feature Is Even Creepier Than I Expected

The “Siri Recap” feature that Apple announced in September is finally available in a developer beta, and I’ve spent the last 24 hours with the feature turned on. It’s even more unsettling than the “Live Rewind” feature that launched at the same time. It listens to all my conversations, and produces summaries that are both helpful and deeply creepy.

I have a button in the watch’s Control Center that can turn the recapping abilities off, but if I forget to do so, Siri listens to everything. I’ll get a recap of my entire evening, presented in roughly hour-long chunks, including things I would have completely forgotten I had even heard about.

The recaps somberly mention silly memes my kids were laughing about, and make major bullet points out of offhand remarks from brief conversations. If a conversation sticks to a single topic, I’ll often get a reasonably good summary of it, with specific facts and numbers highlighted; but just as often, Siri will get confused and mix up several topics or completely mishear a name or phrase.

Apple has four features that it considers part of “audio intelligence":

Music recognition, better known as Shazam. We’ve had a version of this on the Apple Watch for a long time now, although it has some improvements and now identifies music automatically.

Sound recognition, which can notify you about doorbells and babies crying. A version of this launched in 2020 as an accessibility feature.

Live Rewind, which gives you an on-wrist transcript of the last 15 seconds of detected speech.

Siri Recaps, which summarizes entire conversations for you to read on your phone.

Live Rewind had the flashiest demo from the Apple event: A server rattled off the day’s specials at a restaurant, and then the Apple Watch-wearing diner checked his watch to see a readout of exactly which dishes had just been mentioned. The utility is both obvious and kind of unnecessary: Why wouldn’t you just ask the server to repeat the list while they’re standing right there?

I haven’t found myself using Live Rewind, except out of curiosity about how the feature works. I discovered that it doesn’t pick up song lyrics very well, and also that by the time I think to check what was just said in a conversation, more than 15 seconds has passed since the part I was unsure about. I haven’t yet found a reason to use it for real.

But Siri Recaps? Those are both useful and unsettling. I enabled the feature, and decided to test it out later. But since it was on, it dutifully listened in as I picked up my son from school and gave him an update on an ailing family member’s health. We stopped by the library, and along the way we chatted about a variety of things: holiday travel plans, library policies, and the possibility of humans living in space in the future. Siri was listening to it all.

At least for now, the feature is only available in a developer beta, so sign up for that now if you want to try it. You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 (or Ultra 4) and an iPhone 16 or better, excluding the 16e. (I have a 16 Pro, so I'm good.)

After you're updated to 27.3, go into the Watch app, tap Siri, and turn on Siri Recap. You can set a schedule for when it should listen (for example, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., if you want it on for the work day but off for the evening). You'll need to set a passcode on your watch, and you'll be guided through a step to upgrade your audio connection. The control center on the watch will have a button you can use to turn Siri recaps on and off at will. To read your recaps, go to the Siri app on your phone.

But still: I feel weird publishing the contents of these recaps, because they do contain things that people said to me in what they assumed was a private setting. I had the feature on when I attended a choir practice, and Siri recapped the brief chats I had with other choir members before and after practice. (Interestingly, it did not recap any of the quiet conversations I had with fellow sopranos while the tenors were rehearsing their part. I’m not sure if the watch was unable to hear us over the music, or if Siri is programmed not to listen when music is being played.)

Because speakers aren’t identified, it seems Siri doesn’t know what to do when there is a disagreement. A human note-taker would jot down that Person A made a point in favor of something, and person B made a point against. But when my son and I disagreed about how likely space colonization might be in the future, the recap didn’t reflect the separate positions that were put forth. It summarized the conversation as including “debating the feasibility and timeline of human space colonization and asteroid mining,” which isn’t exactly accurate, but close enough.

When it comes to the content of the discussion, the recap notes a bullet point of “skepticism regarding permanent space colonies within the next 100 years.” It didn’t include my reasons for being skeptical, and didn’t mention my son’s opposing viewpoint at all. If I were using this recap to jog my memory of the conversation, it wouldn’t be all that helpful.

Details are sometimes egregiously incorrect. After a discussion about a family member’s health, the recap had notes on the prognosis of “father.” The family member we discussed is not anybody’s father. Names in general seem to be a problem; I recommended a book to my son, and the recap includes notes about the content of the book, but not its title. The book’s author appears in the introduction to the recap (sort of a summary of a summary), but not in the content of the recap itself where the book is mentioned.

I should probably turn Siri recaps off. It seems wrong to let people chat with me without letting them know that their conversation is being ... well, not technically recorded, but basically recorded.

But it’s so tempting to leave it on so that I can review my day. Some of the details in the recaps are useful, like the dates that were discussed as options for a holiday party. The recaps will be deleted in about a week (unless I save them to the notes app), so if I want to remind myself of a conversation a few days ago, I should be able to scroll back through my recaps and find it.

I would be a fool to rely on the recaps, though. The most important points of a conversation are often left out; Siri doesn’t know what’s actually important, and there’s no way to guide it as to what to pay attention to. Specific details can be wrong, as I mentioned. There’s also no way to control when a “conversation” starts or stops, unless you are turning the recap feature on and off from the watch.

And there’s more: Not only are names usually omitted (wait, who did she say I should ask about that project?), the few identifiers that make it into the recap, like names of events, are often wrong. Subjects of discussion are often conflated in really unhelpful ways: My husband mentioned paying for certain course registrations for one of our children, and later I talked to that child about an unrelated exam. The recap got all of these things mixed up with each other and was wrong about pretty much every detail. About all the recap could usefully do is to remind me that something about AP U.S. History was discussed. Reading the recaps can be like reliving your day entirely in the passive voice.
